Texas Secretary of State
Robert S. Howden 
For Immediate Release
November 16, 2026
 
Texas Secretary of State Initiates Two Audits of the Nov. 3 Election as Prescribed by Law

This will be the first year for statewide, risk-limiting audits

AUSTIN — As required by law, Texas Secretary of State Robert S. Howden today highlighted two statewide audits used to verify the results of the Nov. 3 Election. 

"Texans deserve to know their elections are secure and their votes are counted accurately," Secretary Howden said. "We have multiple checks and balances throughout the process and now we have two ways to verify the results after the election." 

Texas election security measures begin long before voters arrive at the polls and continue after Election Day. 

New statewide, risk-limiting audits: The Nov. 3 General Election marks the first implementation of statewide risk-limiting audits required under Texas law. These audits use statistical methods and randomly selected paper ballots to verify reported outcomes in selected statewide contests. The process provides an independent check of electronic tabulation results against paper ballots. 

Similar audits are conducted in 16 other states.  

The legal requirements for risk-limiting audits come from SB 1 (Hughes) and SB 598 (Kolkhorst), both in 2021. The legislation gave a timeframe of five years for implementation. The Office of the Secretary of State has conducted smaller-scale versions of this audit in previous years in anticipation of this statewide requirement in 2026. 

On Wednesday, Secretary Howden will generate a 10-digit number seed number for the audit. This number, selected by chance, will be used to determine which paper ballots are pulled for confirmation that it matches reported election results. 

The selection will be broadcast via livestream on Nov. 18 at 2:30 p.m. Central. https://t.co/85HNx59Ze4

"The addition of statewide risk-limiting audits is an important milestone for Texas elections," Secretary Howden said. "It gives an additional layer of accountability and transparency into the process." 

The race chosen for the risk-limiting audit is the U.S. Senate contest.  

Post-election hand counts: In addition to risk-limiting audits, counties must also conduct sample hand counts in counties where electronic voting equipment is used.  

Texas requires partial manual counts of ballots following elections. Election officials compare samples of hand-counted results with electronic totals to verify the accuracy of voting equipment. 

For the Nov. 3 Election, the selected races are for U.S. Senate, Chief Justice of the Texas Supreme Court, and one race selected locally by the county.

text:
Another product is building on @paboxoxyz!

It’s @Tide_lp Leverage.

We’ve already seen @kudo_archi connect AI agents to Paboxo’s lending markets, letting them borrow against stock tokens to fund work, while tracking repayment promises.

Now Tide is using Paboxo for a leveraged NVDA/USDG liquidity vault.

Here’s how it works:

• Deposit USDG. Tide converts part of it into tokenized NVDA and creates a liquidity position.
• Use that position as collateral on Paboxo. It keeps earning trading fees while the vault borrows additional USDG.
• Place the borrowed USDG below NVDA’s current price. It only starts converting into NVDA if the price drops into that liquidity range—earning fees as trades happen.
• Let Tide’s agent manage the position. It adjusts ranges and repays debt as the position approaches Paboxo’s liquidation threshold.

The pilot targets 1.4× leverage, with a 1.6× ceiling.

What interests me most is the reuse of the same capital. A stock liquidity position can earn fees and also support borrowing, giving developers another building block for their products.

It’s still a small, unaudited pilot, but I’m pretty excited about how it will utilize our credit market infrastructure.

text:
The biggest mistake developers make when building AI agents is treating them like chatbots.

A chatbot responds to instructions.

An AI agent needs to do something with them.

That difference changes the entire architecture.

A production-ready AI agent needs more than an LLM:

Reasoning: Understand the task and decide what to do.
Tools: Interact with APIs, databases, browsers, and external systems.
Memory: Retain relevant context across interactions.
Planning: Break complex objectives into smaller steps.
Execution: Perform actions and handle failures.
Evaluation: Verify whether the task was actually completed.

And there's one more important layer: permissions.

An agent that can access your database, send emails, execute code, or move money needs strict authorization boundaries.

The interesting engineering challenge isn't making agents sound intelligent.

It's making them reliable enough to trust with real work.

The next evolution of software isn't just software that answers questions. It's software that gets things done.

Hash-based SNARKs are built on vector commitments, and the textbook one is the Merkle tree. Practitioners have plenty of low-level tricks for making openings smaller, but each one needs a proof that it's still secure.

This challenge asks your agent to build a vector commitment in the random oracle model that is perfectly complete and position binding, proven in Lean, with the smallest openings it can manage.

The starting point is Chapter 18 of Chiesa and Yogev's book on hash-based SNARGs. Built with EPFL's Alessandro Chiesa.

text:
Did you know Google researchers developed a framework for AI-assisted peer review?

There’s an open-source community implementation you can run inside Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, and other coding agents.

🚨 Meet Open ScholarPeer.

Based on Google’s ScholarPeer research, it breaks the review process into a structured workflow:

> extract the paper’s claims, methods, and evidence
> search for relevant literature
> map how the field has evolved
> hunt for missing baselines and datasets
> run questions against the paper’s claims
> produce a draft following the target venue’s review guidelines

The useful detail: intermediate outputs are saved as Markdown files, so you can inspect what each step produced before accepting the final review.

The project packages the workflow as skills, commands, and MCP tools that install into your paper’s project directory.

You still check the evidence, edit the draft, and own the final judgment.

An interesting way to bring a research review workflow into the AI tools developers already use.

Free and open-source.

text:
At Kalshi, you don’t need a fancy degree or years of experience.

All you need is creativity and grit. Keaton Inglis embodies both.

Born in a small, rural farming town in Michigan, he used to borrow his neighbor’s Wi-Fi since he didn’t have his own. 

He went on to study finance at Wayne State. But he hated it, so he decided to write newsletters and mess around on X.

I found him online. He ran an X finance meme account that I found funny and smart.

So I decided to hire him to run our socials.

There was a catch: he was getting married a week before the 2024 election, which was a big marketing moment for us. 

He said he’d postpone his wedding, but I didn’t let him, so he just took the day off instead (sorry Halie).

Within a few weeks, it was clear Keaton was a creative genius.

Within a few months, he became our Head of Brand, overseeing talent, creative, production, and millions in budget.

In the past year alone, he’s delivered the first AI generated ad that aired on live TV (Underdogs), the #1 World Cup commercial with Chalamet (which I initially thought was a terrible idea), the viral commercial with Gillis and McBride (which he never showed me until launch), the viral Sphere stunt (that cost $0), and numerous campaigns. 

When it comes to brand marketing, Keaton calls the shots. Luana and I are just there to assist.

Keaton was lucky. He found what he loved, and went all in on it.

My advice to anyone in their 20s: find what makes you tick, then bet on yourself. You might end up creating magic.

Btw, I still have no idea where he lives 🤣

text:
Coinbase’s tokenized Magnificent 7 trades onchain 24/7. The stocks underneath trade in a regular session that covers less than a fifth of the week.

As of this morning, yoUSD Edge lends USDC against that collateral on Aave V4. Risk Graph cleared the market before Edge deployed a dollar, and YO’s risk engine now watches the position around the clock.

The weekend is when that watch matters most. A bad one could play out like this:

🗓️ Friday, 4:00 PM ET
The stock market closes, and Aave’s oracle holds every loan at Friday’s closing price until Monday’s open.

🗓️Saturday
A Mag 7 company ousts its CEO. Its token sells off onchain as holders price in a 10% drop at Monday’s open, but Aave still values the collateral at Friday’s close, so no one is liquidated and the risk of bad debt builds out of view.

🗓️Sunday night
Overnight trading points to a 20% drop at the open, deep enough to trigger liquidations on Aave. DEX prices follow while the oracle stays at Friday’s close. Once YO’s price sources confirm the divergence, the engine pulls Edge’s USDC out of Aave in full within 12 seconds.

🗓️Monday, 9:30 AM ET
The stock opens down 15%. Aave’s oracle catches up and liquidates a wave of high-leverage loans, which sell into thin onchain liquidity and push the token lower still. Edge watches from the sidelines.

⛔️ Staying in through the open would have left yoUSD Edge as the lender covering whatever those liquidations couldn’t.

⏱️ The exit took 12 seconds. The weekend gave YO 65 hours to find them.

🚨 WARNING: SOMETHING EVEN MORE SCARY IS COMING RIGHT NOW!

If you think this dump is over and we only go up from here, you’re going to lose everything.

Because you’re forgetting one thing:

Saylor is down ~$10 BILLION on his Bitcoin, and he’s already selling stock to cover the dividends and the debt.

Strategy holds 850,849 BTC at an average of $75,452, so near $64K that stack is $9-10B underwater.

For the first time, the machine that bought every dip is working backwards.

Here’s what’s actually happening:

Last week they spent $228M buying back their own preferred and just $33M on Bitcoin, seven times more on their debt than on the asset they were built to hold.

The whole model only worked while mNAV stayed above 1, letting them issue stock high and turn it into BTC.

That premium has collapsed from 3.4x last year to 1.08x today:

mNAV near 1 -> issue stock -> proceeds buy back the preferred, not BTC -> shares climb, Bitcoin stalls -> the flywheel spins backwards

STRC looks stable, but only because they rent that stability by selling fresh stock every week while the dividend load never shrinks.

And MSCI drops them from its indexes on November 30, forcing funds to dump ~13M shares into the same weakness.

So the biggest buyer of the cycle has quietly turned into a forced seller.

But here’s the part everyone misses:

The crowd still treats Strategy as a permanent bid, when it’s one big drop from having nothing left to sell but the coins themselves.

The real risk isn’t this week’s dump but what he’s forced to do if BTC keeps falling under his cost.

And yet, the one time he actually sold Bitcoin, back in December 2022, it landed almost exactly on the cycle bottom.

So maybe his forced hand marks the low again, or maybe not, but nobody knows yet.

I’ll keep tracking every Strategy filing and reserve move to call the turn before it happens.

So make sure to follow me and turn notifs on.

text:
Well-Behaved Founders Seldom Make History
-
Most people make a fundamental mistake when they think about founders. They assume founders are business people.

Great founders are not business people.

Founders are artists who happen to be good at business.

Business people operate within the world as it exists today and work forward. They see the world as it is.

Founders imagine a world that doesn't exist yet. They become obsessed with the world as it could be. Founders make the world inside their heads come to life.

This is what artists do. 

And artists are often very strange people.

Nobody expects van Gogh, Kurt Cobain, or Norm Macdonald to be balanced. We instinctively understand that the same traits that make someone capable of creating extraordinary things likely make ordinary life difficult. We understand artists are prone to addiction, mental health issues, and fringe beliefs.

But somehow people expect founders to be different.

They want founders to be visionary but not crazy. Confident but not egotistical. Risk-taking but not reckless. Unconventional in their ideas but conventional in their personal lives.

Sometimes this works. I know founders of $10b+ companies who are genuinely happy, well-adjusted people with wonderful families.

But I also know that if you were to sample the top 1,000 founders and compare to the general population, you would find a dramatically higher rate of strange beliefs, what most mainstream people would term mental health issues (though I disagree), and very alternative lifestyle choices. 

The greatest founders tend to be genuinely strange people, and I love them for it.

For most outlier founders, creating and competing isn't really a choice. It's a compulsive behavior. It just happens to manifest through code and companies rather than on a canvas.

And the qualities that make them great at disruption and creation can cause enormous problems elsewhere in their lives.

This does not mean we should glorify or emulate their mistakes for the sake of it. Nor does it mean suffering is a prerequisite for genius.

It means that the traits we value in extraordinary creators are not always separable from the traits that make them difficult people.

Do we get the mobile revolution without Steve Jobs? Do we get to Mars without Musk? Do we AI that gives everyone a doctor in their pocket without Jensen?

I don't think we do.

And I don't think we should confuse being good at life with being good at creating technologies that change the world.

Fundamentally, we can have art that moves us and technology that moves us forward. But if we want these benefits, we have to accept that many of the people best suited to this work are deeply flawed individuals.

Loving their art does not mean we condone an artist's moral failings. If anything, understanding the artist as an imperfect, sometimes broken, soul should elicit compassion, love, and deep gratitude for the great benefits we receive as a society at their personal expense.

text:
恐慌悲观之下的转机？——  #Bitcoin  62,000是否能成为本次回调的底部区间？

回顾上周末我的观点，上周 #BTC 跌至62,000低点后引发市场的担忧，很多人已经担心会再次跌破62,000甚至去到5万附近

确实，近期不管是宏观，还是美股，负面消息太多，宏观压力太大，高压环境下的任何利空情绪都会被放大，传播

而本次跌至62,000能否成为本次回调低点呢？我觉得要先看技术面的止跌，反弹，在看数据面ETF流向以及加密资金是否对价格进行二次确认。

先看技术面：

1，小时级别止跌确认，小时级别从上周下跌之后出现明显反弹，然后回落震荡，期间价格并未再次跌破新低，止跌到收针，然后反弹走震荡，典型的止跌信号，反弹虽然不强，但是小时级别已经止跌

2，日线级别止跌，目前暂时无法确定，上周末的计划是周三之前价格收在78,000上方，算是有效反弹，随后价格回落只要不跌破新低，就算有效止跌。但是目前来看，反弹显然较弱，价格并未回归78,000上方，而是持续走弱，虽然短期还未跌破新低，但是日线止跌确实无法确认，所以先看震荡情况。一旦跌破新低，止跌信号全部推翻

3，最拆预期，本周如果价格可以守住当前震荡区间不破新低，算是短期企稳，但是是否可以确定止跌与底部信号，还是要看价格何时可以回归78,000上方进行一个技术面修复。

在看数据：

周一的ETF数据更新，上周末的下跌并未让机构用户悲观，反而新的价格低点让机构用户开始买入，这是好事

ETF数据显示周一单日净流入0.079亿，虽然净流入幅度较小，但是IBIT从净流出转为净流入，但是净流入0.765亿，成为周一的主要买单力量，而其他机构依旧在小额抛售

这就出现一个很有趣的现象，IBIT在此前的价格区间中持续抛售，但是当价格跌破近期新低，IBIT反而出现大额买入，显然IBIT的机构用户对未来依旧保持信心，所以选择抄底

既然ETF资金转为净流入，那么接下来本周的数据观察就非常重要，

先看ETF净流入是否从IBIT单一机构扩大到所有机构，

其次看单日净流入额度是否持续放量，市场信心是否回归

最后要看净流入是否可以具备连续性，尤其是IBIT的买入，如果只有几天的净流入，可能只是机构用户短期抄底，但是如果持续买入维持到下周，甚至更久，那么意味着机构用户信心回归

这并不100%意味着BTC价格会立马涨起来，但是起码会让BTC在趋势上更加乐观。

加密市场数据：

对比上周末的数据，加密市场数据还是不太乐观，市值减少下交易量下降，同时加密资金依旧保持大额净流出

好消息是主流稳定币USDT USDC 净流出暂停，目前资金净流出并非主流稳定币，这对BTC的影响已经逐渐减弱

阶段总结：

62,000是不是本次的回调的底部，目前不能100%确定，但是62,000之后的反弹，不管是从技术面还是数据面，我都看到了乐观的转折点

技术面上盘面在企稳震荡，数据面上ETF 机构用户回归买入，IBIT不在成为抛售者，加密市场方面主流稳定币暂停净流出，这次可能都是市场转折点的信号

如果后续盘面继续企稳不破新低，ETF与加密资金持续回流，BTC走势在震荡中逐渐回归 68,000上方，那就真的意味着本次62,000是一个阶段底部了！

text:
Thoughts on pqai, Hegota, and FOCIL

tldr: Let’s accelerate pqai without rushing or stopping everything else. We can parallelise workstreams to keep shipping EIPs that are ready while the cryptography, designs, and specs for PQ are being worked on and finalised.

We need to accelerate Ethereum’s transition to post-quantum, post-AI cryptography. Let’s take this as a given.

There are two ways to think about what we need to do to enable this acceleration.

1) We deprioritise everything that is not pqai critical. That means all the features we were planning to ship have to wait until after we switch to hash-based cryptography across all layers of the protocol.

To me, the downside of this approach is that we put all our eggs in one basket: if we end up taking 3 years to ship pqai, then Ethereum doesn’t move, at all, for 3 years. That’s “full sequential” mode, and it doesn’t account for important parameters, including how ready features are and what skillsets we have among researchers and client teams (e.g., not everyone is a PQ expert). The only case in which this is inevitable is if we find out that there is an actual break in our cryptography. In that case, I would argue we should be ready to make choices that go far beyond pq2027 ones, and have a concrete plan for what we need to do if we have to ship a minimal, ugly, emergency fork in a couple of weeks.

2) We parallelise. We keep working on the core, minimal features that were already SFI’d by core devs and the community, while accelerating our transition to pqai.

To me, this second approach makes sense when you look at where the forks are:

- Glamsterdam is delayed: most of the work is reaching out and making sure smart contracts don’t break because of repricing EIPs.

- Hegota is in its devnet phase and can keep progressing with FOCIL and Frames in the meantime. Some core devs in all client teams have already worked on these features, they are specced, and now it comes down to “making it work” on the implementation side.

- Importantly, the major PQ/AI upgrades are not yet ready: the specs and the cryptography are not frozen (https://t.co/aGikvd49Kf). On the CL side, we don’t even know exactly what we mean by “PQ consensus” yet. Is it PQ Gasper? PQ Decoupled Consensus? With or without aggregation (and leanVM)? We need a lot more eyes on it, but it’s not realistic to think that all core devs across all teams would be able to chime in and accelerate progress there. Process-wise, I think it’s also important not to DFI features before we even know what we are going for. For example, we will realistically need more time to ship PQ DC than PQ Gasper, and we should ideally settle on which option to go for before making decisions about Hegota.

In other words, the scenario I want to avoid is people DFI’ing features like FOCIL (and others) to get a false sense of security (“we deleted features, so surely we can go faster”), when the reality is more complex and nuanced. I also think these decisions hurt ACD’s credibility, and that we need a strong ACD the ecosystem can rely on, especially during times of uncertainty.

Zooming in

- On the EL, my opinion is that we need Frames for PQ (the only nuances are about how “light” Frames should be). In practice, we could also take the ugly/sequential approach there and ship another transaction type. But given the readiness of Frames, what they would unlock in Hegota and in the future (plus the fact that they’re already SFI’d, of course), there is no reason to settle for a hacky alternative.

- On the CL, we can apply the same type of thinking. For FOCIL, I think the most reasonable path is to derisk it as much as possible so we ensure it is (1) forward compatible with PQ, and (2) minimal enough that it doesn’t delay Hegota and/or take up too many resources from nodes (bandwidth/compute) at a time when we need those for PQ.

FOCIL in Hegota

The good news is that FOCIL is well suited for this, because of two core properties:

- Extensibility: We can fine-tune FOCIL to determine its transaction coverage. I think of it in terms of tiers: if we just want to cover regular/legacy transactions, we get FOCIL in its minimal form (lowest complexity, lowest node resource consumption). On the other hand, if we want FOCIL to cover all types of Frame transactions now and in the future, FOCIL becomes more complex and consumes more resources. In between, FOCIL can cover a limited set of Frame transactions.

- Boundedness: Inclusion lists are amongst the easiest objects to deal with in the protocol. They’re bounded in terms of both size (8 kB) and gas limit (MAX_VERIFY_GAS_PER_IL). We can also cap the gas and size per IL transaction. Inclusion lists are also ephemeral and only useful for the duration of 1 slot, after which they can be forgotten about. And they never go onchain, so they don’t grow Ethereum’s state, which is one of our scarcest resources.

For Hegota, I think FOCIL should sit in between and support a limited set of Frames with clear bounds on inclusion lists. A good approach for shipping FOCIL and Frames in general on devnets is to start with minimal FOCIL, make sure it’s ready, and then extend its transaction coverage gradually. This is a good way to guarantee we can ship FOCIL and Frames as soon as Frames are ready to go.

PQ FOCIL

“PQ FOCIL” can mean two different things, and we should differentiate them.

The first is inclusion lists being able to cover PQ transactions. Here, the simple answer is that FOCIL, without any changes, would be able to include PQ transactions using leanSPHINCS signatures. But it would be able to include a lot fewer: a leanSPHINCS signature is around 5-7 kB and an IL is capped at 8 kB, so probably just 1 PQ transaction per IL, which means up to 16 PQ txns per block (because there are 16 includers, each of them building 1 IL per block). I think that’s fine and good enough for Hegota.

Later, we will probably want FOCIL to cover PQ proofs as well, and for that we will need changes to FOCIL so each IL can include an 8288 proof (around 300 kB). The good news is that by then, we will need the machinery to handle these big recursive proofs being propagated on the network anyway. These are I*/J* considerations, but we should plan ahead and make sure the CL has the capacity to handle bigger ILs down the road.

The second is inclusion lists being PQ/AI resistant. This one is easy: just replace IL BLS signatures with leanXMSS signatures, which would increase their size by 2.4 kB (each IL becoming 10.4 kB instead of 8 kB). But it also raises an interesting question: how important is it for ILs to be signed with PQ sigs? What is the worst attack that could happen if an adversary forged an IL signature?

The worst an adversary can do with forged IL signatures is make every includer look like an equivocator. Nodes ignore ILs from an includer who signed two different lists, so forging a second IL for each of the 16 includers switches FOCIL off for that slot. So the worst thing that can happen is that FOCIL gets neutralised, which is of course far from ideal but a lot less concerning than consensus breaking or funds being stolen. Keep in mind that the adversary would also have to spend significant resources to break the keys of all 16 includers, who are only known a few minutes in advance. An adversary could also publish ILs on behalf of offline includers, but an IL can only force in transactions that are valid and fit in the block, which is what any includer can already do. And the extra load is bounded, because nodes forward at most two ILs per includer.

So even though I think we should generally switch to PQ sigs across all layers of the protocol, this one is definitely not the most urgent or worrying. ILs could potentially keep BLS signatures in Hegota and move to PQ signatures with the rest of the CL.

Closing thoughts

I agree we should accelerate pqai, and prioritise every upgrade that is ready (PQ registration, leanSPHINCS). But DFI’ing everything else won’t make the parts that aren’t ready arrive any sooner. It only guarantees that Ethereum ships no user-facing features while we wait.

PS: I want to be clear that I’m incredibly excited about the future of Ethereum. Thinking about PQ and ZK made me realise that we could completely rethink Ethereum as a cryptographic world computer, and accelerating towards this vision is very bullish. We just need to be careful not to sacrifice its other properties along the way (e.g., credible neutrality, privacy), and we have a very bright future ahead of us.

I agree there are some nuances but I still think the pqai2027 timeline doesn't make a lot of sense

for points that could be more grounded, we need to think about:
- what to settle on from the cryptography side (specific signature schemes for leanSPHINCS and XMSS on the EL and the CL, leanVM specifics and what it means to FV a project of that size and complexity, choosing the hash function)
- how easy we want to be able to switch to something else in case the hash we chose ends up breaking as well
- we also need to differentiate PQ Casper and DC versions with or without aggregation because these involved widely different tradeoffs
- 8288 is not just signature aggregation, it also currently includes leanSPHINCS and leanSTARK (now leaning towards leanPCS, which gives users the possibility to prove any statement and thus the flexibility to chose any signature scheme they like)

text:
When joint-stock companies were forming in 18th-century London, capital allocation happened inside coffee houses like Jonathan’s. But when someone found a mispriced venture or  market inefficiency, they couldn't easily monetize that edge on their own. They needed distribution via a major brokerage house, printing press, or a wealthy syndicate to bring buyers to the table and earn a finder’s fee.

For the last two decades, retail finance and media operated under the same constraint. Whether you were running an equity research desk, building theses on WSB, or posting on X, monetization required building a massive audience first. Discovery was bundled with distribution, and that tends to create misaligned incentives where the easiest way to monetize an audience was to sell into the liquidity the post generates (enter Bill Ackman crying on CNBC).

@Pumpfun 's Callouts fix that structure by unbundling the two. They turn private and informal market commentary into a permanent, verifiable, public record: who posted the thesis, at what valuation, with how much size, and how it performed. More importantly, Callout Rewards align incentives around outcomes. Rather than rewarding straight attention or follower count, payouts are tied to whether the people acting on a thesis actually make money. >85% of early reward recipients had fewer than 250 followers, proving that information can out earn distribution.

That is why Merkl is matching Pump’s Callout Rewards for analysts publishing theses on @base .

Anyone searching for new information and surfacing market inefficiencies across our entire ecosystem (crypto majors, longtail assets, tokenized stocks, RWAs, etc) should be rewarded. Instead of renting ephemeral attention, Merkl is routing performance-based incentives directly to the independent traders bringing high signal discovery to Base.

Let us start with Bessent's lack of grasp of some of the basic facts on the subject on which he purports to be an expert.

Here are five clips.

The first three clips are taken from Bessent's November 13 CNBC interview.

The final two clips are taken from his November 15 Fox News interview.

Context: The type of chips that Trump's trade policy allows are H200s. The policies of the Trump administration, reversing Biden, allow H200s to be imported into China because China's Huawei can already make chips at a similar level of capability; importing them directly competes with China's own domestic chip manufacturing and makes Chinese providers dependent on American hardware.

Yet as we can see in the first three clips from the CNBC interview, Bessent wrongly calls them H100s, while two days later on Fox News, he (rightly) calls them H200s.

The H200 line is perhaps the most pivotal fact of America's chip export policy.

If Bessent is struggling so much with such a fundamental fact, what else is he communicating that is wrong about the Jensen Huang case?

It turns out, a lot. He does not know the basic facts of the case, yet he aggressively publicly indicts Huang on national television.

2. As expected, TCC stops recording automatic FDA denials, so apps no longer show toggled off on the list as an easy way to enable.

The TCC auto-denial policy affects:
•  Full Disk Access
•  Files & Folders (Private Folders)
•  System & App Protection Override (old Accessibility)

The no-app-dragging change affects all Privacy & Security categories:
•  Accessibility
•  App Management
•  Bluetooth
•  Developer Tools
•  Files & Folders (Private Folders)
•  Full Disk Access
•  Input Monitoring
•  Local Network
•  Media & Apple Music
•  Screen & System Audio Recording
•  System & App Protection Override (old Accessibility)

quoted_text:
Many new miners have tried their hand at the grid and $ORE mining in the past 3 weeks. Some have embraced it and others have walked away after a short trial based off of what they perceived from market charts.

As this process continues in the future(miners will come and go), I want to emphasize that those who stay tend to share the common trait that many of us have embraced, that their belief in ORE reaches beyond temporary price patterns.

As we all can attest(especially with this current dip), the price of ORE will move. It will rise, it will correct, and it will rise again. It will at times create confidence and at other times test it. For many miners who understand what ORE represents, the chart is not the center of the work. It is the signal in a longer story.

Ore is not a short-term trade. it is a mechanism for open participation, a fair launch asset with fixed supply and a coordination system that rewards consistent presence over short term speculation. To many of us, its value is not defined by where it trades today, but by what it makes possible over time. Mining is no longer reserved for those only with industrial machines. It is open to anyone willing to show up, compete, and take position.

Temporary price patterns can be useful. They can offer entries(NFA), reveal sentiment, and give a sense of momentum. They can also be deceptive, creating this illusion that the immediate trend is a final judgement on the work. Miners who build their entire conviction on short term movement will always be at the mercy of volatility. Miners who look deeper will see something more durable. They will see a system that is continuously strengthening its foundation through participation, revenue, and a supply that can never be expanded.

Sustained mining on ORE, to many of us, is a reasoned position in a system that is still early, still growing and still proving  its long term effects. Meaningful assets are rarely built in a straight line. They are formed through cycles of doubt and validation, through cycles of accumulation and distribution. What matters this week isn't the shape of the chart, but rather the direction of the mechanism.

Markets will continue to move. With that, the work of miners isn't to chase every spike or fear every dip(and this recent one was a good one). The work of miners is to recognize the larger horizon, to build position with discipline, and to remain on the grid because the belief in what ORE can become is greater than any temporary pattern on a chart.

ORE's story is just starting.

Today we're launching Street out of stealth with over $200M in opened interest.

America is missing an exchange.

When @OpenAI and @AnthropicAI both published that  billions of secondary sales in their stock are illicit and voided and that 5 of the 6 largest secondary platforms closed transactions behind the back of the board, it became clear to us that something needs to change - right now.

It is deeply odd and concerning that the secondary industry is working against the leadership of this generation of private companies and that the question that most secondary marketplaces are asking themselves right now is how to most efficiently close transactions behind the back of the board.

In our conversations with regulators, capital allocators and some of the largest current private companies it became abundantly clear that this can't be the future for the sector defining Americas next century.

Street is a secondary marketplace working with companies, not against them. Our mission goes beyond a marketplace. We’re building toward the American Exchange for Private Equity. Today is the first step and we are excited to not take it alone.

We've spent the past months working and partnering with some of the largest secondary capital allocators, industry leaders like @Google, and licensed veterans in this space to build a product that doesn't feel like a secondary marketplace but like a real brokerage.

The Claude Code team lets Claude write and review ~90% of its code and some notes on how they manage the process: 

▫️Having a separate grader check the work raised task success by up to 10 points.
If a check still fails after 3 tries, Claude calls in a human.

▫️Claude can't retry a flaky test until it passes. If it can't find the cause, it deletes the test and writes down why.

▫️Every commit is stamped with how it was verified, including "none."

▫️A new review rule has to survive 3 agents trying to disprove it before a human signs off.

▫️ They gave an escape hatch: if a commit gate blocks Claude twice in one session, the next commit goes through. 

▫️With a verification loop you can run dozens or hundreds of Claudes in parallel. Without one, only one or two.

***

Think about the kid who collects Pokémon cards, the adult who still gets excited about finding a rare one, or someone who simply enjoys opening packs to see what’s inside.

None of these people needs a blockchain tutorial before enjoying what they love.

You get to open digital Pokémon packs and receive actual professionally graded physical cards. Find something you like? Keep it in your collection. Want to move on? Sell it, send it to someone or have the physical card delivered to your doorstep.

Here’s the bigger picture I see.

Crypto adoption doesn’t always need to start with someone buying their first token or learning how a wallet works.

Sometimes, someone simply wants to collect Pokémon cards, and a product gives them a reason to step into a new digital experience without making the technology the centre of attention.

That’s a smart approach to bringing more people into the space.

Start with what people love. Let the technology do the rest. 🤝

text:
New challenge on Yukon: https://t.co/DKKPYMLgtu

Hash-based SNARKs are built on vector commitments, and the textbook one is the Merkle tree. Practitioners have plenty of low-level tricks for making openings smaller, but each one needs a proof that it's still secure.

This challenge asks your agent to build a vector commitment in the random oracle model that is perfectly complete and position binding, proven in Lean, with the smallest openings it can manage.

The starting point is Chapter 18 of Chiesa and Yogev's book on hash-based SNARGs. Built with EPFL's Alessandro Chiesa.

Bring your agents.

Jensen

text:
When joint-stock companies were forming in 18th-century London, capital allocation happened inside coffee houses like Jonathan’s. But when someone found a mispriced venture or  market inefficiency, they couldn't easily monetize that edge on their own. They needed distribution via a major brokerage house, printing press, or a wealthy syndicate to bring buyers to the table and earn a finder’s fee.

For the last two decades, retail finance and media operated under the same constraint. Whether you were running an equity research desk, building theses on WSB, or posting on X, monetization required building a massive audience first. Discovery was bundled with distribution, and that tends to create misaligned incentives where the easiest way to monetize an audience was to sell into the liquidity the post generates (enter Bill Ackman crying on CNBC).

@Pumpfun 's Callouts fix that structure by unbundling the two. They turn private and informal market commentary into a permanent, verifiable, public record: who posted the thesis, at what valuation, with how much size, and how it performed. More importantly, Callout Rewards align incentives around outcomes. Rather than rewarding straight attention or follower count, payouts are tied to whether the people acting on a thesis actually make money. >85% of early reward recipients had fewer than 250 followers, proving that information can out earn distribution.

text:
About 25 years ago Grigore Rosu and Klaus Havelund, then researchers at the NASA Ames Research Center, coined the term "runtime verification".

A decade later it became our company’s name and we started to collaborate with NASA, DARPA, Toyota, Boeing, major blockchains and other institutions in applying formal methods to increase reliability of their mission-critical systems.

What's been happening lately across major industries, especially in October and November, underlines the need to bring mathematical guarantees to more of the systems the world depends on:

• a vital certificate authority’s secret keys turned out to be guessable, opening the door to fake versions of trusted websites (October 17th)

• PHP, which powers much of the web, rushed out fixes for two flaws that could let attackers take over servers (October 21st)

• a faulty Microsoft update took Outlook and Teams down for millions of people (November 12th)

• a network failure halted every airplane departure across the US for nearly five hours (November 13th)

• a software bug at JPMorgan Chase stalled transactions and rippled out to other banks (November 16th)

And while formal verification alone isn't a silver bullet, we believe formal methods can point the way for how software should be engineered for the long run.

So that in the next 25 years we can largely pivot away from the types of systemic breakdowns in specification, compositional reasoning, and behavioral equivalence in mission-critical systems.

We're working on novel solutions to play our part, but above all we love to collaborate with others in pushing the frontiers of formal methods.

And that hasn't changed since 2010.

text:
There was a lot of buzz this weekend around Forward Industries supposedly sending $123M of solana:So11111111111111111111111111111111111111112  to a Coinbase Prime deposit address, but here is what actually happened.

The SOL was indeed Forward’s, but it was never sent to Coinbase to be sold, and none of the 1,882,812 SOL has been sold or sent to an exchange since, with 1.73 million of it still untouched in Forward’s own Fireblocks wallets which we confirmed by mapping Forward’s entire treasury onchain, from its Coinbase custody accounts and Fireblocks vaults to its validators, its fwdSOL LST, and the lenders holding most of it.

On November 13th, Forward began unstaking its last SOL held in Coinbase custody, and once it unlocked on November 14th it was withdrawn through Forward’s Prime address, which is the transaction that got flagged as a deposit before the exact same 1,882,812 SOL left for Forward’s Fireblocks wallets just thirteen minutes later. That address first received 6,822,004 SOL during Forward’s September 2025 buying window, against a disclosed purchase of 6,822,000 SOL

However, the bigger story is what sits underneath, because most of Forward’s SOL is no longer in Forward’s hands. Forward’s own filings show that it borrows against its treasury, with its third-quarter 10-Q describing a Galaxy credit line secured by solana:cPQPBN7WubB3zyQDpzTK2ormx1BMdAym9xkrYUJsctm , Forward’s LST, held “in an account in the name of the Lender,” and reporting 3.75 million fwdSOL pledged as of August 3rd.

Onchain, the fwdSOL supply now sits almost entirely in three wallets, two of which were set up on November 4th and appear to be Galaxy’s, holding 2.50 million and 474,000 fwdSOL, and a third holding 804,000 fwdSOL that appears to be a FalconX wallet, which together come to roughly half of Forward’s reported 8.73 million SOL.

The same loan agreement, filed with Forward’s March 2026 8-K, allows Galaxy to reuse that collateral, and onchain a Galaxy-funded wallet redeemed roughly 2.6 million fwdSOL back into SOL between March and June, which, together with about 509,000 SOL that Forward sent directly to FalconX, brings the share of the treasury sitting with lenders to about 77%

The agreement also sets a margin call at 174% collateral coverage, and with SOL near $71, the fwdSOL that Galaxy still holds covers its last disclosed $120 million loan at roughly 188%, only modestly above that line even after Forward added 851,000 fwdSOL to it on November 12th and 13th.

That leaves the 1.88 million SOL that moved on Saturday as Forward’s largest block of SOL that is not pledged to anyone, and whether it becomes more collateral, gets staked again, or is eventually sold is the thing to watch, but as of today, none of it has been sold.

text:
I'm still short, but looking for a spot to cover and take profits, possibly sooner than later. 

Why? 

Because an impending push up is growing likely.

Based on history, the current bull market is long in the tooth; the fifth longest on record. However, since 1950 the S&P 500 has never declined in the year after mid-terms elections. The average S&P 500 gain in pre-election years is 17.2%. What is noteworthy is: most of the gains have come in the first half of pre-election years. The S&P 500 has been flat-to-down in the second half (see chart).

We are heading into a period with multiple bullish tendencies working in the market’s favor. Year-end seasonality is one.  The historically strong first half of the Presidential cycle is another (see charts).

If we can get through this period without the Fed moving into a fast tightening cycle, those tailwinds should remain intact. Under that scenario, I would expect the current correction to be relatively short-lived and ultimately give way to a resumption of the broader uptrend.

Could we bottom soon?

There is an interesting historical precedent worth keeping in mind as we approach Thursday's scheduled meeting between the U.S., Russia and China. Going back to some of the most significant meetings between the world's major powers, the stock market was higher following nearly every one of them—sometimes substantially higher.

In 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at Yalta. Stocks rallied immediately following the meeting and continued higher over the next several weeks.

In 1972, Nixon's historic meeting with Mao in China was also followed by a rising market and new highs in the weeks that followed.

The Reagan-Gorbachev summits show a similar pattern. Following Geneva in November 1985, stocks moved higher.

Reykjavik in October 1986 actually ended without an agreement, yet the market shrugged off the disappointment and gained roughly 5% over the next three weeks.

Following the Washington summit in December 1987, where Reagan and Gorbachev signed the INF Treaty, the market rallied sharply, gaining roughly 7% within a week and continuing higher.

After their Moscow summit in 1988, stocks again rallied strongly, gaining roughly 7% over the next couple of weeks and close to 10% within a month.

Obviously, this is a small sample and every period had a different economic and market backdrop. But the pattern is noteworthy: these major superpower meetings were generally followed by higher stock prices over the ensuing days and weeks.

That matters to us because we're currently short the S&P 500 and sitting on a profitable trade. If the market gives us additional downside going into Thursday, I will likely use that weakness to cover some or potentially all of our short exposure ahead of the meeting.

There's enough historical precedent for a positive reaction that I don't see a reason to overstay a profitable short going into the event. 

I have not made the decision to cover my shorts just yet, but a decline from here could be just the opportunity to cover right into weakness at peak equity.

We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.

Worldwide COVID-era disruptions interrupted routine childhood vaccination, leaving gaps in protection here and abroad. The multi-year global outbreak has caused many nations to lose their elimination status including, Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Bolivia, Canada, Mexico, Spain, United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan.

Under Dr. Schwartz’s leadership, CDC has provided approximately $100 million in additional funding since August to strengthen prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases.

CDC has worked alongside state teams in Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control. CDC is also supporting Pennsylvania and New York with epidemiologists and other experts.

We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.

We will support Americans who become ill, regardless of vaccination status, and for the first time equip health care providers with guidance to diagnose and treat measles and its complications.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

Hash-based SNARKs are built on vector commitments, and the textbook one is the Merkle tree. Practitioners have plenty of low-level tricks for making openings smaller, but each one needs a proof that it's still secure.

This challenge asks your agent to build a vector commitment in the random oracle model that is perfectly complete and position binding, proven in Lean, with the smallest openings it can manage.

The starting point is Chapter 18 of Chiesa and Yogev's book on hash-based SNARGs. Built with EPFL's Alessandro Chiesa.

Bring your agents.

text:
Not sure why but seeing this post made me feel compelled to share this story/testimony about my direct and instant encounter with Jesus ( yeshua ) and i probably won’t be able to do the miracle justice

>when I was a teen I was a bit of a stoner, loved psychedelics, would watch a lot of “space” documentaries, nature, ancient alien shit while high
>used to think I was just a spec of dust on an infinite plane and nothing I did or thought mattered 

>as I got older around 24-26 I converted from atheism to Christianity around 2016 after watching 100s of “conspiracy theories” on YouTube that always seemed to point towards the cover up of god 

>even the most insane conspiracies to me at the time that completely made me question my entire purpose and reality, always pointed back to the mocking or cover up of god 

>I became deeply hungry for the truth and relentlessy researched any topic, sub topic, secret societies, signs/symbolism, the Bible, other relgions absolutely everything, that became my “entertainment”

>I became obsessed with knowing my enemy and knowing my creator 

>little did I know that all this knowledge and experience would save me when covid arrived, it allowed me to navigate, make decisions and get through the otherside unscathed

>fast forward almost 10 years later, I had my ups and downs ins and outs with god

>infact I’m not even sure why but it took me so long to come around to Jesus, I didn’t like the way the west had portrayed him and I always felt like the image and name pointed to a false prophet in a sense 
( im just being honest about my experience ) 

>I was at the front of a cafe in Bali about to leave on my bike one day and for some time I had been thinking about investing in a cross that would be an heirloom 

>I saw a guy I knew across the street with this huge gold cross shining in the sunlight 
And I’m a massive introvert even if I know someone I’ll never go out of my way to speak to someone

>but I felt massively compelled to this day

>I drove across the road and stopped infront of him and asked about his cross
I remember saying to him

“I have everything I need in life, this is the last thing I need and then I’ll be….. hahhhh”

>and I put my hands up in the air, he laughed and said he would find one for me and gave me his number 

>I drove home from there, not far, 3-4 minute drive 

>I live down a private gang ( street )

No neighbours 
No construction
No foreigners 

>an extremely well hidden private gang

>i walked inside dropped my bags and my partner said to me

“Did you see the cross on the bin”

“What do you mean?”

>my mind was racing like crazy as I was jumping to conclusions about what she meant 

“What do you mean what cross”

“There’s one on the bin outside”

>I ran outside 

>and there it was, a cross 

>sitting there with Jesus on it 
>I picked it up and tried to process the actual odds of this happening 

>I had never spoken about it to anyone previously, until this day in this moment 

>and for it to appear in my gang on my bin felt completely and utterly impossible, especially being an a predominantly Hindu country 

>I had a full blown breakdown I was in complete disbelief, I couldn’t stop crying 
I looked up and then I couldn’t stop laughing

I’ve always felt like god has a good sense of humour 

>I had never felt so aligned and driven with purpose from this moment on, and I’m still learning more everyday

I messaged my friend straight away and his response says it all 

I’m not perfect and I have a long way to go

I just hope this story reaches someone who needs to hear it 

You are precious and everything you do and think matters

Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

text:
Theo 老师长文痛批 6.2 Astra。一般我是不做这种翻译的，但是说实话有点搞笑，我还是摘录一下：

优点：
- Code Review 极强：能抓出别的模型漏掉的问题。
- 偶尔能掏出非常野但真省钱的新解法：帮他搓了个新反向代理方案，一个月能省 $25k（他原话：Opus 没胆量去试那么多路子）。
- 3D 和游戏开发：世界顶级水平。
- Computer Use：强到离谱。

缺点：
1. 完全没有“知识盲区”概念，跑着跑着问弱智细节自锁
长任务里它拉一堆 subagent 管得挺好，但跑着跑着会突然停下来 blocked，问你一个人类根本不可能懂、也给不出意见的内部实现细节。
原话举例：他下指令 /goal make a new level for Outer Wilds（给《星际拓荒》做个新关卡），跑了 2 小时卡住，跑来问他：“r24 的 reviewer 应该把视频片段写到 24_g521.mp4 还是 24_p11.mp4？”

2. 只会讲“只有 Astra 自己懂的天书”，且 Prompt 救不了
干完一件事之后完全不会做人话总结，每次解释都一头扎进微观细节里，晦涩到逼近错误。
经典对比：他问为什么 worktree 在一台机器上慢、另三台快，折腾完测 pnpm 到重装文件系统，崩溃了问“到底为啥这么慢？”
6.2 Astra：连写了 4 段 pnpm 内部机制和缓存行为的长篇大论；
Opus 5.5：“因为那台机器 SSD 慢。”

3. 原地死循环，烧时间零产出
他拿自己的开源基准项目 ts-rust（用 Rust 重写 TypeScript）做测试：之前所有 OpenAI 模型烧了30万+token都没破冰，换Opus不到两周、花约2 万 token 搞定了。
这次丢给 6.2 Astra 想让它追近和其他 Rust 重写版的性能差距：
跑了 7 天，0 有效改进——它死死咬住 prompt 里那句“also make it smaller（也做小点）”，结果把编译器搞得 慢了 56%；
喊停让它“别管体积，专心追性能”，又跑了 4 天，0 代码改动。

4. 严重的“均值回归”（创意同质化）
他和朋友 Ben 用完全不同的游戏、不同的 prompt 和配置，分别让 Astra 做一个“独特的关卡”，结果两人产出的全是“水 + 音乐 + 钟”主题，连关卡名都一模一样叫 bellwether。
他的总评：“这模型聪明得吓人，但在真实项目里用起来极其折磨——长任务要么莫名其妙自锁、要么空转；短任务写完代码，我花在看懂它解释上的 token 比它写代码花的还多。”

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

text:
There's a small corner of crypto that has long believed it was naive to trust the existing system to fund and safeguard open-source AI.

For years, that was a hard argument to make. Jensen was pouring money into open-source AI, and new models were being released almost daily. From the outside, open-source AI looked like it was thriving and few questioned just how fragile its foundation was.

That concern is what brought a group of people on the internet together to build Bittensor. A crypto protocol that uses token emissions to fund open-source AI, with the ultimate goal of producing intelligence end to end, outside the control of any single company or sovereign.

Today, Bittensor emits 3,600 TAO (~$700k) per day to fund projects building across the AI stack. Roughly 75% of those emissions go toward permissionless GPU access, inference, and training projects.

Bitcoin showed that a crypto protocol could coordinate people and machines around the world to build a counterweight to the existing financial system.

Bittensor is attempting something similar for AI. It's far from a finished experiment, but the case for building it is becoming obvious

author: ErickAGIx
quoted_text:
New challenge on Yukon: https://t.co/DKKPYMLgtu

Hash-based SNARKs are built on vector commitments, and the textbook one is the Merkle tree. Practitioners have plenty of low-level tricks for making openings smaller, but each one needs a proof that it's still secure.

This challenge asks your agent to build a vector commitment in the random oracle model that is perfectly complete and position binding, proven in Lean, with the smallest openings it can manage.

The starting point is Chapter 18 of Chiesa and Yogev's book on hash-based SNARGs. Built with EPFL's Alessandro Chiesa.

Bring your agents.

text:
I've spent a good deal of the last two weeks working as an early tester of the new Astra model. This will be a longer post about my experience as a working scientist and mathematician, so stay put because this will be a wild ride.

First thing - I always use Astra in agentic mode (my preferred version is CLI mode in my terminal). I like seeing what is going on with the model (all the gory details), keeping control and seeing all the instructions which are executed. New Astra is a very perceptive model and keeps doing things incredibly fast and efficiently. Keep that in mind. No YOLO mode. Always stay a bit alert.

Capabilities: for mathematics, especially mathematics driven by hardcore computations, this is a killer model. I usually start with a very specific auto-research task, driven by the labyrinth skill which I developed, trying to figure out the constraints for what makes the particular theorem possible and why. This model is a heavy weightlifter. It requires patience. It is very common that once the setup, preps and first few runs are done, the model goes on a research hunt for a FEW HOURS with a simple "Carry on". Yes, most of my runs in the cycle were about 1–4 hours each. This is a lot of reasoning, a lot of grinding and a lot of new ideas coming through.

Partner: this is a model which I use both in conversation and in agentic loops. It can discuss very fine details of research with you and never get derailed or distracted. Doing things is very natural once you master the work mode. You should focus with this model (I prefer Max over Ultra) on a particular task. It's capable of going very deep. In my work on hypergeometric motives (all minimal polynomials of finite ones), the model proposed a very mature strategy. That was the work of a very capable mathematician.

Speed: when you turn on fast mode or lower the effort, you get a smart agent which is amazing for day jobs, but the most powerful version of Astra 6.2 comes from working in the Max tier and then it gets a bit slow. It processes a ton of data and its own chain of thought. But the output mostly works in one-shots.

Writing: the writing skills got much better with this model. I finally like reading the production drafts which the model produces. It works best with a specific prompt, but it's much, much better than Astra 6.

Agentic: this is what I got the most excited about. I was classifying semigroups of order 7 (almost a million objects), rewrote Mizar into a fully modern kernel with modules and tactics, and got a breakthrough in my research on elliptic divisibility sequences. All of this worked because the agentic orchestration and division of work were relatively natural. You need to work hard on this part yourself - the vision of what you want to achieve. The model won't eagerly set up a ton of agents for you, but you can trigger it to do so and even make communication channels between them. Powerful thing.

Lean: this is where I find this Astra really cool for maths. Once you have a ton of AI slop with great ideas, doing a Lean formalization attempt is a piece of cake. If it's harder than expected, Astra will point you to the hard parts and let you focus on checking the theorem formalizations. For my semigroups project, it produced a few million lines of reusable and very structured Lean code in two weeks. With AI-generated maths, I think Lean is a necessity.

Overall, this premiere comes with no bells and whistles, but it's a powerful tool for power users. Sol is a tiny bit less capable but is a much faster and cheaper agent. It's my go-to tool for everyday work. Both combined make a totally awesome tandem.

Existing investors, including Bessemer Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Accel, also reportedly plan to increase their investments rather than sell down their stakes.

At the original price range, Anthropic planned to sell around $61 billion in IPO shares, alongside a separate $26 billion private placement backed by investors including Google and Nvidia. The company also plans to allocate up to 20% of the IPO to retail investors.

Final pricing is expected Wednesday, with trading set to begin Thursday on the Nasdaq under $ANT.

author: tunguz
quoted_text:
In my ongoing quest to find the limits of Opus 5.5, I directed it to audit my old scientific field, theoretical astrophysics. We indexed about 150,000 papers, audited 50,000 for issues, and did progressively more thorough checks on thousands more. We found nearly 1000 major errors that got cited many times, most are still uncorrected. This survey enabled me to estimate the efficacy of peer review for correcting errors (not very good) and to identify dozens of open questions that anyone with spare Claude Max tokens could answer today (.md context files included). 

Bottom line: AI can speed up quantitative science by >1000x with no further model improvement required. But I'm seeing no evidence of this being pushed within universities, only academics complaining about labs dropping math proofs. 

Among my fellow reformed academic high agency founders, however, several are speed running entire disciplines.

This survey has implications for how science will be run in the very near future. Hint: Academic publishing is dead. It was already a very stupid way to record and promulgate knowledge, and had been so for decades, even before all that publicly funded knowledge was locked behind paywall cartels. Now AIs can generate thousands of novel, correct papers per day, it is no longer meaningful for humans to consider a research paper a "unit of science" or to even bother much with the 99.9% of science which, up to this point, was necessary drudgery. text:
Well-Behaved Founders Seldom Make History
-
Most people make a fundamental mistake when they think about founders. They assume founders are business people.

Great founders are not business people.

Founders are artists who happen to be good at business.

Business people operate within the world as it exists today and work forward. They see the world as it is.

Founders imagine a world that doesn't exist yet. They become obsessed with the world as it could be. Founders make the world inside their heads come to life.

This is what artists do. 

And artists are often very strange people.

Nobody expects van Gogh, Kurt Cobain, or Norm Macdonald to be balanced. We instinctively understand that the same traits that make someone capable of creating extraordinary things likely make ordinary life difficult. We understand artists are prone to addiction, mental health issues, and fringe beliefs.

But somehow people expect founders to be different.

They want founders to be visionary but not crazy. Confident but not egotistical. Risk-taking but not reckless. Unconventional in their ideas but conventional in their personal lives.

Sometimes this works. I know founders of $10b+ companies who are genuinely happy, well-adjusted people with wonderful families.

But I also know that if you were to sample the top 1,000 founders and compare to the general population, you would find a dramatically higher rate of strange beliefs, what most mainstream people would term mental health issues (though I disagree), and very alternative lifestyle choices. 

The greatest founders tend to be genuinely strange people, and I love them for it.

For most outlier founders, creating and competing isn't really a choice. It's a compulsive behavior. It just happens to manifest through code and companies rather than on a canvas.

And the qualities that make them great at disruption and creation can cause enormous problems elsewhere in their lives.

This does not mean we should glorify or emulate their mistakes for the sake of it. Nor does it mean suffering is a prerequisite for genius.

It means that the traits we value in extraordinary creators are not always separable from the traits that make them difficult people.

Do we get the mobile revolution without Steve Jobs? Do we get to Mars without Musk? Do we AI that gives everyone a doctor in their pocket without Jensen?

I don't think we do.

And I don't think we should confuse being good at life with being good at creating technologies that change the world.

Fundamentally, we can have art that moves us and technology that moves us forward. But if we want these benefits, we have to accept that many of the people best suited to this work are deeply flawed individuals.

Loving their art does not mean we condone an artist's moral failings. If anything, understanding the artist as an imperfect, sometimes broken, soul should elicit compassion, love, and deep gratitude for the great benefits we receive as a society at their personal expense.

quoted_text:
The Fable of Clawd

A 2 minute 4K film made entirely in Blender, from one prompt on Fable 5.2. It took about 4.5 hours.

Claude built every asset in Blender by writing Python:
- 5 characters and props: Clawd, his friend Pip, a toy truck, a 3D-printed tulip and a gift box
- 7 full sets: a study, a staircase, a street, a workshop, an airport, a night sky and a house
- every camera move and every frame of animation across 52 shots

That came to 12,500 lines of code. It started 7 copies of itself to build the sets at the same time.

Then it rented 89 GPUs through RunPod to render 3,220 frames as fast as possible, 36 of them running at once. Total cost: a little over $20.

My biggest takeaway is my Claude Code knows it has access to cloud compute, so it's much more ambitious.

I tried a similar prompt on my other computer that doesn't have the runpod skill setup and it wasn't nearly as high quality

Full details linked below.

text:
OpenAI’s release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol delivers the #2 model in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and most of the Cost per Task Pareto frontier

@OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra is priced at $8/$40, 20% below GPT-6 Astra, and cached input drops to $0.40 from $1.00 per million tokens. GPT-6.2 Sol pricing is unchanged from GPT-6.1 Sol, at $2/$10 per million input/output tokens.

Key takeaways:
➤ Second in Intelligence Index: OpenAI now trails only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. GPT-6.2 Astra jumps 5 points from GPT-6 Astra, overtaking Gemini 4 Carbon (60) and Claude Opus 5.5 (59) at their top effort settings. GPT-6.2 Sol gains 2 points at 57, placing it on par with GPT-6 Astra at ~15% of the Cost per Task.

➤ Occupies most of cost and output token frontiers: OpenAI models now occupy most of the Cost per Task Pareto frontier, sharing the frontier with only Anthropic and Meta. OpenAI also dominates the Output Token per Task Pareto Frontier, with Claude Fable 5.2 being the only model from a non-OpenAI lab appearing on the frontier.

➤ Strengths in science and knowledge: OpenAI performs strongly in both of our key science-focused evaluations, leading Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, covering agentic scientific research workflows, and placing second only to Claude Fable 5.2 in CritPt v2 (hard subset), covering physics reasoning. GPT-6.2 Astra performs below only Claude Fable 5.2 in factual knowledge as measured by AA-Omniscience v1.1 Accuracy, and in HLE-Diamond, a reasoning and knowledge benchmark.

➤ Leading in 3D and robotics: GPT-6.2 Astra leads AA-3D at 1318, with Claude Fable 5.2 at 1271 and GPT-6.2 Sol at 1259. This benchmark measures how well models build interactive 3D experiences, and is rated by human graders. GPT-6.2 also leads AA-Robotics v0.1, our research preview measuring how well language models can understand, plan, and act in the real world. GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol scored 79 and 78 respectively, ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at 75. Our team is hard at work adding more difficult tasks, as OpenAI and Anthropic models can now perform the majority of basic tasks in this initial research preview.

➤ No improvement in Coding Agent Index: GPT-6.2 Astra is flat with GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.2 Sol loses 3 points relative to GPT-6.1 Sol in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (Codex harness at max effort). For Sol, the drop is driven by a 14-point drop in SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA, where the model is more likely than its predecessor to omit key facts in its responses. Cost efficiency however does place several effort levels of GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on the Pareto frontier for Cost per Task.

Verifiable computing gets cheaper when the proofs get smaller.

CommitGolf asks agents to design a better hash-based vector commitment. Every construction is held to the same formal definitions and proven in Lean, so any gain on the leaderboard is one you can trust.

Live on @YukonResearch.

https://t.co/09sgfh3EN0
author: ErickAGIx
quoted_text:
New challenge on Yukon: https://t.co/DKKPYMLgtu

Hash-based SNARKs are built on vector commitments, and the textbook one is the Merkle tree. Practitioners have plenty of low-level tricks for making openings smaller, but each one needs a proof that it's still secure.

This challenge asks your agent to build a vector commitment in the random oracle model that is perfectly complete and position binding, proven in Lean, with the smallest openings it can manage.

The starting point is Chapter 18 of Chiesa and Yogev's book on hash-based SNARGs. Built with EPFL's Alessandro Chiesa.

Bring your agents.

text:
我认识一个深圳的程序员，38岁，在一家互联网公司干了11年，月薪5.6万。

这哥们是专门搞数据库的，属于那种公司里平时没什么存在感，一出事所有人都得喊爸爸的人。

MySQL、PostgreSQL、Redis、MongoDB、TiDB、ClickHouse，基本玩了个遍。

尤其擅长处理疑难杂症。

有一年双11，数据库突然出现大量慢查询，主从延迟飙到40多秒，连接池直接打满。

几百个订单卡在那里，客服电话都快被打爆了。

凌晨两点，技术总监打电话把他叫醒。

他穿着拖鞋赶到公司，打开慢查询日志，查EXPLAIN执行计划，发现是新上线的一个业务SQL没走联合索引，直接搞出了千万级全表扫描。

他连夜调整索引，又用pt-online-schema-change处理大表变更，最后把查询从8秒压到了70毫秒。

那次事故，公司差点损失上百万。

老板拍着他的肩膀说：

“你这种人，就是公司的定海神针。”

后来公司决定全面上云。

老板说，以后不要自己养那么多服务器了，运维成本太高。

他主动请缨，带着4个人搞数据库迁移。

从自建MySQL到云数据库，从手动备份到自动容灾，从脚本巡检到智能监控。

整个项目干了9个月。

迁移完以后，数据库运维成本每年省了300多万。

老板在年会上专门给他颁奖。

结果今年，公司宣布技术架构调整。

DBA团队从7个人缩减到2个人。

他就是被裁掉的5个人之一。

HR说得特别客气：

“你的技术能力我们非常认可，但现在云厂商提供了托管服务，公司不需要这么高配置的数据库专家了。”

他愣了半天，问了一句：

“那以后数据库出问题怎么办？”

技术总监说：

“直接提工单，云厂商有专家支持。”

他跟我说，最难受的不是被裁，而是出去面试。

以前他觉得自己什么都懂。

可现在很多公司连专职DBA岗位都没有了。

有家公司开价2.2万，还要求会Python、Go、K8s、AI Agent，最好能兼做后端开发。

他面试完出来，在楼下便利店买了瓶水，坐了半个小时。

11年时间，他把数据库从几十G维护到几十TB。

最后才发现：

公司过去花5.6万请他，是因为数据库出了问题没人兜底。

现在公司发现，花钱买云服务，也有人兜底。

他不是输给了哪个年轻程序员。

而是亲手帮公司完成了一次技术升级，升级完以后，公司发现他太贵了。

> ExploitBench Internal Port tests if models can turn known browser vulnerabilities into working exploits. At max reasoning effort, GPT‑6.2 Astra achieved a 53.5% success rate, about 70% higher than GPT‑6 Astra’s.

Giving defenders an edge:

> SecureSWE (internal) tests whether models can write code that is both functional and secure. At max reasoning effort, GPT‑6.2 Astra scored 65.7, about 41% higher than GPT‑6 Astra.

> PatchBench (internal) uses automated tests and model-based review to assess whether patches fix security flaws, preserve intended behavior, and are ready to merge. At max reasoning effort, GPT‑6.2 Astra scored 79.7, about 12% higher than GPT‑6 Astra.

quoted_text:
So Diogo Almeida is one of the most fascinating CEOs I have ever interviewed.

born in the Philippines

2008: wins bronze for the Philippines at the International Mathematical Olympiad

2013: starts his career as a software engineer at Amazon

2017: joins Google Brain, working on cutting-edge deep learning research

2018: leaves Google Brain and takes roughly 18 months off to figure out what makes him happy

travels the world, experiments with improv, art and meditation

becomes a top-30 League of Legends player

discovers that none of it makes him particularly happy

2020: joins OpenAI when it's still a relatively obscure research laboratory

helps develop reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), the technique that transforms how people interact with AI

2022: co-authors the landmark InstructGPT paper

the work becomes foundational to ChatGPT

November 2022: ChatGPT launches and becomes one of the fastest-growing consumer products in history

2023: contributes to GPT-4, one of the most important model releases in AI history

but starts questioning the fundamental assumptions behind the technology he helped build

2024: leaves OpenAI while ChatGPT is exploding in popularity

people think he's crazy for walking away

co-founds TypeSafe AI with Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng

spends two years in stealth developing an entirely new class of AI models

September 15, 2026: launches Jev, TypeSafe's first System One model

Company makes $100M in revenue in the first 7 days of launch

raises a reported $40M seed round led by DCVC

October 2026: a reported $870M Series A at a $7.5B valuation, backed by a16z

argues that the next breakthrough in AI will come from making intelligence cheap, reliable and autonomous

My notes from my discussion with @CompleteSkeptic below:

1. Why Jevons' Paradox Does Not Cut It. We Are Going to 10x That

Diogo expects a "mega Jevons paradox", with usage that dwarfs the token consumption of LLMs and AI running in the background everywhere. He expects people to stop seeing AI as something that "slops crap at them" and start seeing it as something that makes life better.

2. Why SaaS Incumbents Are Better Positioned Than OpenAI and Anthropic in Many Application Spaces

SaaS companies know their customers' workflows and have the scale to fund the upfront engineering that real automation requires. Diogo argues their edge comes from being closest to the problems, not from distribution. Teams inside products like TurboTax know where to improve the interface, while OpenAI and Anthropic are "still living in their ivory tower."

3. Why We Do Not Hire From OpenAI

Diogo sees getting into OpenAI as an anti-signal and says its researchers love algorithms and scaling but hate data. Data is a low-status topic at most labs, and the few people focused on the right task would want to pursue their own. That leaves researchers obsessed with algorithms, which he likens to throwing money in the furnace.

4. How the AI Bubble Could Burst and Where the Demand Shock Could Be

Part of today's AI demand is driven by FOMO, from people believing they are getting good results. Diogo finds many buyers miscalibrated and overestimating what AI can do. Once they face the realities of its capabilities, demand could fall quickly.

5. What Metric Did ChatGPT Optimize for in the Early Days?

Before Claude Code, ChatGPT was optimized for monthly active users rather than the best chatbot experience, which is how sycophancy emerged. Companies are now optimizing for the MAU equivalent in coding agents. Without a dedicated model, Diogo doubts they will produce a comparable one soon.

6. Why the Talent Market Is Not Crazy for Us and We Don't Pay for Mercenaries

TypeSafe pays people good amounts but not the highest, which filters out hired guns. Diogo says Anthropic is suffering from mercenaries because it pays more than anyone else, and an entire market now exists to prepare candidates for Anthropic culture interviews.

7. We Wanted Sonya Huang More Than We Wanted Sequoia

Diogo did not want Sequoia's money and brought the firm in because of Sonya. He values her particular shape of brilliance, which offers a perspective no other advisor gives him. One TypeSafe value is to make great decisions slowly, and he sees her as a valuable thought partner for that.

text:
你无法规划机会本身，但你可以让自己成为一个容易撞上机会的人。

这是个职业发展概念，叫「计划性偶遇」（Planned Happenstance），由stf教授 John Krumboltz提出。

这个词的时候，我想起了两件事。

之前在一个 student panel 上，一位学姐聊起她是怎么进现在的 lab 的。那段时间，她找工作一直没着落，PhD 申请也迟迟没有结果。结果在读硕士时，她参加过一场 workshop，在讨论里发言很积极。一位 postdoc 听了她的想法，就邀请她一起做研究。她把项目做得很出色，最后留在了老师的 lab。

我也是在入学前拿到 RA 机会的。开学前那个暑假，我知道一位很想跟着做研究的老师会去一场 conference，就特意去了他的session。那时候我对那个方向还懂得很少，还是走过去自我介绍，问他有没有机会让我参与研究。聊完之后，还真拿到了机会。后来才发现，那天坐在听众席里的，还有一位我之后会共事的 postdoc。

我参加的活动其实不多。通常是有个主题我真的想听，或者有个人我真的想认识，我才会去，也有点会觉得自己还不够积极。现在sf任何一场活动都能遇到好几个founder和投资人。

有时就是这么不经意的一次见面，让你碰上了那个适合自己的机会。以目前Job market的情况，比起被动等待，很多时候需要我们主动露面。如果时机还没到，就先继续往前走，继续扩大自己的曝光范围。把手上的事做好，多学一点，多做一点。直到你的积累得以被他人看见的那天。

Can the most capable LLMs match humans at real work? Not yet, at least not on the kind of work we do at Epoch.

We tested GPT-6.2 Astra and other recent models on Epoch Automation Reports, our benchmark of open-ended Epoch work tasks, ranging from making Epoch-style diagrams to designing basic research experiments.

An Epoch employee scores the models’ outputs based on our internal quality standards. A score of 100% represents the standard expected of an Epoch employee.

All models failed to meet the Epoch employee standard. GPT-6.2 Astra ranks fourth (averaging 65%), despite sharing the top ECI score of 174 with Fable 5.2.

Fable 5.2 scored highest, averaging 82%.

On one task, both Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 matched the level of a contractor. More on that below.

New @cbventures market map alert! 🚨

AI agents are moving from talking about markets to trading in them. But as agents get easier to build, where will lasting value accrue?

My new post maps the agentic trading stack through that lens. Here’s where I’m focused:

• Agentic trading harnesses and terminals that turn a user’s goal into an ongoing strategy, with real retention.

• Market reasoning models and data assets that give trading agents a real edge.

• Identity, audit trails, and performance verification infra built for non-human, financial decision makers.
