author: myanTokenGeek
quoted_text:
有朋友问，为什么说王安电脑是黄仁勋的前车之鉴？

确实这个类比不难想到。王安生在上海，哈佛的博士，工程师出身，自己创业，把王安电脑从计算器做到文字处理机，又做到商用电脑，八十年代中期，已是一家三万人、营收三十亿美元的公司，1992年8月，申请了破产保护。两个人都是华人工程师，都把一家公司带到了一个时代的最前面。王安电脑的教训有好几层，个人电脑没跟上，债越背越重，可我觉得最该引以为鉴的，是任人唯亲。

王安电脑有一位董事Peter Brooke，据他自己回忆，1963年他就进了董事会。2010年，他在计算机历史博物馆的口述历史里说，王安一直想让儿子接班，他和另外几位董事觉得Fred Wang还没准备好，有两位董事为此辞职。他自己留了下来，因为觉得欠王安很多，想继续劝他。他还特意说，分歧不在技术，也不在市场，这些王安懂得很多，分歧在管理结构。可王安握着过半的投票权，辞职的走了，留下的没劝动，Fred Wang还是当上了总裁。1989年，公司债台高筑，王安不得不撤掉了自己的儿子。

英伟达这边，11月16日，《纽约时报》引十几位现任和前任员工的话说，黄仁勋的女儿Madison，头衔是物理AI产品营销的高级总监，实际上已经成了他的幕僚长，参加高管的季度会，向董事会汇报，在营销和公关上说话很有分量。报道里有几件事。今年2月，黄仁勋临时不去新德里，改派副总裁Jay Puri，准备的电话会上，她因为准备不足斥责员工，Puri对她说，你不吼，我就能回答。不到半年，Puri离开了原来的位置。3月的开发者大会前，她又因为CUDA之父Ian Buck打算即兴做媒体简报，斥责了他。她跟CFO Kress（现在的临时CEO）在机器人投资上屡有冲突，牵涉她丈夫、副总裁Nico Caprez的几笔数据中心交易，也跟高管们起过争执。员工估计，三年里有十几位关键高管，因为不愿跟她共事而离开，人力资源部门曾安排她每周接受辅导。同一篇报道里，同事也说她聪明，是有天分的营销人，对外很能代表公司。

其实这些冲突，反映出三种矛盾。

首先，权力不在位置上。今年5月的股东大会文件写着，他的女儿和儿子都不是高管，也不直接向他汇报。纸面上，这都是真的；报道说的，是纸面之外。写公司论的时候我说，岗位是一个位置，持职责。权力落在位置上，才有一个可以问的地址，做了什么决定，凭什么，错了谁担。一位高级总监，做的是幕僚长的事，她的分量不来自头衔，来自她是谁的女儿。这样的权力，找不到地址去问。

第二种矛盾，是谁敢说不。Puri的头衔比她高，跟了黄仁勋多年，也只能说一句，你不吼，我就能回答。跟她争，像是在跟CEO争。写公司论的时候我说，问的人不因问而受罚。可在这样的结构里，不同意的人，最后多半只剩一条路，走。王安电脑是两位董事辞职，英伟达是十几位高管离开。隔了三十多年，换了公司，换了人，异议出去的方式还是一样。

第三种也是最麻烦的一种，是两份忠诚撞在了一起。报道说，她护父亲护得很凶，去年牵头请来了一家危机公关公司，外界报道Megaspeed和Alice Huang的时候，又是她力主强硬回应。做女儿的护着父亲，是人之常情，不该苛责。可公关的位置，是对公司负责的，写公司论时我说，公司对各方，要说同一个故事。一份对家里的忠诚，放到一个本该对公司负责的位置上，连她自己也很难分清，此刻护的是公司，还是父亲。

报道里引哈佛商学院的Yoffie教授说，任人唯亲几乎总是个坏主意。我同意，但想把理由说准。坏，不在于亲人一定不行，她也许确实很能干。坏在这个结构里，行不行，没法被如实地知道。附和她的，分不清是服她还是怕她；离开的，多半不说为什么走；她自己听到的，越来越多是顺着说的话。写反对造神那篇我说，被供起来的人，得到的服从越来越多，判断自己对不对所需要的信息，却越来越少。放在一位CEO的女儿身上，也一样。写制衡那篇我说，没有制衡，也就没有保护。人力资源的辅导不是没有，可它改的是她的脾气，不是她的位置。现在父亲走了，她面对的，是十几位匿名同事的说法，不是一次有来有回的、公平的评价。

据报道，她还在原来的岗位上，给她留多少权力，要由临时CEO Kress来定，而Kress，正是跟她起过冲突的人之一。这一题怎么答，是判断层的事；可答的人，最好不只是跟她有过冲突的那一位，理由也该说得出来，经得起问。她不该因为姓黄而上，也不该因为姓黄而下。该被问的，是她做过的事，放在一个说得清的位置上来问。

王安想把公司交给儿子，最后亲手把儿子从那个位置上撤了下来。任人唯亲的坏结局，从来不只落在公司身上，也落在那个被放上去的孩子身上。位置不是传家的东西，孩子也不是父亲的延续。

text:
英伟达营收翻倍，下季度还要涨，毛利率为什么反而要降？

黄仁勋辞职后的第一份财报 $NVDA 营收 1,158 亿美元，同比增加了 103%，下季度指引 1,300 亿美元，但毛利率却要从 74.8% 降到 71% 至 72%。

主要原因应该就是 Vera Rubin 在换代，存储在涨价。

财报中数据中心环比多了 186 亿美元，Rubin 一个平台就带来了近 200 亿，也就是说 Blackwell 等老产品基本没增长，这个季度的增长几乎全靠换代。

Rubin 才刚开始爬坡，财报说现在卖多少取决于能造多少，为此把供应承诺加到了 3,900 亿美元。

而毛利率的下降主要是存储，包括 HBM 在内的存储涨得比英伟达预想的还快，而英伟达已经定好的提价，要到明年 2 月左右才开始生效，再加上 Rubin 刚量产，初期成本也高。

说人话就是成本先涨了，售价还没跟上。

所以把这份财报和 8 月的电话会放在一起看，从明年初开始 Vera Rubin 和 Grace Blackwell 的 AI 服务器大概率都会涨价。第三方报道可能上涨超过 15%。

对买服务器的客户来说，明年初交付的机器会更贵。对英伟达来说，其实就是把存储上涨的成本转移给了用户，所以按管理层 8 月的估计，2028 财年的毛利率也只会回到 72% 至 73% 左右，仍低于这季的 74.8%。

PS：小伙伴们感兴趣的中国业务也有阐述。英伟达 8 月给指引时，没把来自中国的数据中心计算业务收入算进去，结果这季向中国交付了 24 亿美元的 Hopper。这个出货额差不多相当于营收超出指引金额的三成，至于这批货当季确认了多少收入，英伟达并没有单独披露。

text:
币圈人炒美股的几个恶习，一定要避坑这几个点：

1. 信仰盘
看准一个就以为是比特币，疯狂加仓，从 存储 到 Circle，到最近也有人喊英伟达。其实不管任何股票都有周期，不是所有的成功路径都可以通过早期囤比特币这种信仰盘的方式来复制，这种幸存者是极少的。但币圈往往是被早期囤比特币能发财、囤以太坊能发财的人洗脑，认为只要搞信仰盘就能够赚钱。

2. 只会炒热门票

什么热炒什么。其实美股涨得好的，往往是悄摸摸在偷偷发展的公司，不一定是热门票。
一个票若是热门票，要么是涨到了顶点，要么是博弈面极其复杂，这种参与进去大概率都是韭菜，因为热门票的仓位已经极度拥挤了。
就单看存储半导体，有多少人能真的赚到钱落到口袋里？而消费、医疗和网络安全，很多股票已经破了新高，但因为不在新闻热点上，币圈的人也没有深度覆盖的能力，所以只能跟着热度炒。但炒公司跟炒币不一样，公司是有长期投资价值的，不是说那些冷门的就没有。

比如有一家公司几乎没有人提，半年时间已经稳稳翻倍了，而且几乎没有人提过：维多利亚的秘密，对，就是搞维密秀、卖女性内衣的那家公司

3. 只会炒情绪盘
别的不说，币圈的人炒情绪盘确实是很厉害的。因为炒 meme 和炒山寨币，大部分只要看情绪就够了。

但炒美股，当然炒情绪也是一方面，但大部分时候还是要回归公司的基本价值跟行业逻辑，以及关于估值体系、这个市场交易的拥挤度和资金配置等问题。要考虑的层面，其实要比单纯看情绪面博弈复杂得多，而且看情绪面博弈的胜率和收益比，也没有币圈来得高。

所以要炒透美股，还是要扎扎实实做好基本面研究：对公司的业务、公司本身的估值，以及公司的未来战略和上下游，都要搞清楚。

比如有个公司叫 TBBB，是 Druckenmiller 的持仓，做的是墨西哥的平价超市。其实基本面非常好，但也并不在情绪盘里，这个公司今年也翻倍了，而且走势非常稳，不像科技一样大起大落。

4. 盲目相信 KOL。
当然这点其实并不是币圈的问题了，A 股包括很多股票圈的人也是盲目听着 KOL 就冲进去干了。

但交易其实是自己的，KOL 只能提供一些他的思路。你要知道 KOL 他擅长的是什么：他是短线还是长线？他是交易基本面、情绪，还是技术方向？

如果这都不知道你就盲目跟，你一定会丧失自己的节奏。因为没有 KOL 是永远准确的，也不可能第一时间就告诉你该买多少、该什么时候卖。

我也订阅了很多 KOL，但我从来不会盲目抄作业，而是会把他们的思路吸收和分析，看有哪些是对的，有哪些我认为他们说得不对，我也不会盲目去跟单。

总之，炒美股是一个比炒币复杂得多的事情。炒币赚钱当然牛逼，但不一定能代表炒美股赚钱，特别是个股。

所以大家在看这些美股信息，特别是币圈 KOL 发的时候，还是要对他的观点有一个自己的判断。

“the most contrarian thing of all is not to oppose the crowd but to think for yourself.” — Peter Thiel

I see nine different variations on“who still uses Perplexity?” on this app daily, as if not knowing is some sort of flex. the answer is simple: your lawyer, your realtor, your dentist, your accountant, your kid’s teacher, your e-commerce entrepreneur neighbor, your mom and dad, and countless others. regular people. people who’ve never even heard of Claude Code. the kind of people few others in the Silicon Valley echo chamber are building for.

when I joined the company earlier this year, some brilliant people I’m lucky to be close to seemed surprised. why not hold out for a job at one of the labs? that was the consensus move at that moment. I saw something others didn’t: a company quietly outperforming everyone’s expectations, doing more with less, growing revenue faster than anyone seemed to realize, and building approachable, human-centered products with an incredible level of care. I’ve seen this movie before.

there was a time when it was industry consensus that Apple was dead, and that anyone who was serious about building software was building for Windows or maybe Linux. we all know what happened next. incredible things happen when you keep your head down, ignore the noise, trust the fundamentals, and let genuine customer obsession guide your every move.

everything you’ve seen from this company so far has been a warmup. it is without a doubt the most talent-dense team I’ve ever been part of, and we’re truly just getting started. can’t wait to show you all what’s next.

text:
Patriot Act for AI is coming.

They are going to try to lock down AI from every angle, and keep the best AI capabilities restricted to those on the right lists.

Don’t let it happen. Speak out.

Yes, there are cyber attacks happening everywhere, but it’s temporary.

Engineers and cybersecurity firms have never had more powerful cyber defense tools than they do now.

While bugs are getting exploited, hundreds more are getting found and patched before anyone attacks.

AI is favoring the defense. But the decades of pre-AI code needs to be patched up. This takes time.

I am confident because crypto saw a huge wave of bugs and attacks earlier this year.

Turns out public money systems are the easiest profitable target to attack first.

It was a grueling 4 months or so. Dozens of new bugs discovered daily. DeFi protocols getting hacked daily. Critical patches getting rolled out regularly.

But eventually the dust settled. The teams that were proactive and used AI tools well, managed to patch everything up before attackers get to them.

Of course bugs still get discovered today, but not at the insane pace earlier this year. And the bugs being found are more complex to exploit, which makes them hard to use.

The attack surface for crypto got well hardened by the cyber defenders, and while there is always a threat, hell stopped raining down.

So there is a light at the end of the tunnel.

The rest of the world will harden their software until there’s no more gaps to sneak into.

It’s tumultuous now, but it will end in everything being more secure.

Don’t like them take your rights in the process.

Don’t let the fear give in to invasive government overreach.

Don’t let them steal your right to run code and use AI.

Fear is the enemy, not AI.

Indian law enforcement froze $3M from an innocent Chinese investor after mistaking a crypto bridge for a pig butchering scam. Now an Indian court has ordered Gate to hand his funds to a person they never belonged to.

My analysis of how Indian LE traced through an unlabeled service and wrongly froze @xxxkeym's Gate account:

The case stems from a pig butchering victim who allegedly lost $1.7M of BTC, USDT, DOGE & SOL in May 2025.

Andhra Pradesh CID registered it as Cr. No. 10/2025 and filed a charge sheet in March 2026.

In July 2025, xxxkeym had Gate deposit address 17mpajZ6Nq3dG3T6wUhaXxYF4Qy9HJnYx5 frozen after depositing 15 BTC from 3NcBhqK in the following transaction:
885f3afab562251b222363cf12095e864ddb94636674b01f0cdb05997e5a54a0

This is one transaction Indian LE cites in its notice. 3NcBhqK was funded by xxxkeym's own OKX & Binance withdrawals in Jan 2023 and the coins sat dormant for years until the Gate deposit. 

Indian LE never froze his OKX or Binance accounts, the actual source of the 15 BTC, which tells you how flawed their justification is.

Gate froze his entire account, which held roughly $3M at the time and about $1.5M today.

The Indian court order hands all of it to the complainant.

Gate deposit address 17mpajZ also received two deposits for 15 BTC total in 2025 from bc1pkkwqyxn3rm608ryuqg9hyqna0syq4jx5pxkr7pzg8n3usx6tyqfst5u966, which is also controlled by xxxkeym.

Shortly before the deposits to Gate, bc1pkkw was funded in three transactions by bc1quzwkggdf6ly06mrrnnled0qdr57w770k45n5n7 & bc1qtu66zfqxj6pam6e0zunwnggh87f5pjr7vdr5cd.

bc1quzw & bc1qtu66z were reported as alibarbit[.]bit, the same scam named in Indian LE's press release. 

That was a mistake. Both belong to the Merlin Chain bridge, which is unlabeled in most compliance tools. 

xxxkeym is simply a normal Merlin user trading tokens on the L2. This wrong label is the only place the scam touches his transaction history.

Below is the blockchain data showing each Merlin withdrawal by xxxkeym matched to a BTC payout from those addresses, plus screenshots of the bridge activity.

xxxkeym bridged 50 BTC into Merlin on March 28, 2024, over a year before the alleged May 2025 theft. 

His three withdrawals came out of that balance. I found zero onchain connections between xxxkeym and the theft.

Separately on July 15, 2025 xxxkeym had a 7 BTC private key compromise theft which was reported to local police and also SlowMist was engaged. His stolen funds flowed to Wasabi. 

This is embarrassing incompetence by Indian LE, who seem incapable of reviewing basic blockchain data.

Indian LE, the prosecutor and the judge all signed off on this, Gate froze the account, and LE did a full press release about it recently, while the real victim here (the Gate user) hasn't had access to his funds for nearly 16 months.

My hot take is VASPs need to challenge weak jurisdictions like India, Canada, etc due to repeated negligence in criminal cases.

CEOs are accountable to the market, so they have to be at least somewhat honest, or else the product just doesn't work.

Modern Western politicians are typically liars, but they do need to get elected, so extremely flagrant matters sometimes lead to accountability.

Finally, journos lie for a living, but they lie in packs, all at once, together — the school-of-fish strategy — so it's hard to single one out. Who coulda knew? All that is reflected here. 

Fundamentally, I submit that's what's actually going on. Most people can't keep twenty people in their head, all the journos spreading lies. But they can keep one face in their head. We defended Polymarket for years. 

Through the CFTC fine. Through the FBI raid. Through "new phone, who dis."

Now its markets are live inside https://t.co/MqP2N2Tooz.

Meanwhile Kalshi is in talks to raise at $65B, and Polymarket still hasn't announced its $21B round.

Both started with the same idea: let people trade on what happens next.

Kalshi sued its own regulator and won. Then it kept shipping: 

- Single-stock perps on 50+ companies this month, 
- Indices 
- AI compute futures.

Meanwhile Polymarket sits in the "Predict" tab, next to memecoins and perps, inside the app that destroyed crypto !

One is building an exchange. The other is becoming a feature in a memecoin app.

What hurts is how badly we wanted to believe.

A 22-year-old building alone in a Lower East Side apartment in the middle of a pandemic. The misfit who actually made crypto useful. 

"Shayne is one of us."

We put that story in every thread. We sent it to every friend who said crypto was a scam.

Then it started to derail:

→ "Keep growing and pay a fine." What he reportedly told staff during a $10M stolen-card fraud wave (WSJ)
→ Creators paid to show fake winning trades on cloned versions of the site (WSJ)
→ The compliance chief who flagged the fraud resigned. The US CEO got fired.

Misfits don't run that playbook. 

If you still think "Shayne is one of us", I have a bridge to sell you.

Feelings aside, this is a once-in-a-lifetime case study. Two frontier companies, this close, this different and so comparable:

→ Founders: two MIT math folks vs a NYU artsy Adam Newman type
→ Culture: Alfred Lin's Sequoia vs Dragonfly, Blockchaincap, 1Confirmation
→ Habits: grinding in the office vs company-paid private jets for basketball games

Result = $5B+ vs $1.8B+ revenues

Kalshi isn't a saint. Most of its volume is still sports

But you have to look at where it's going. Prediction markets either become a real asset class or the next casino. 

Kalshi is building toward the first. Polymarket chose the second.

text:
quotrons migration  - what you need to know, and what you need to do (nothing tbh)

today, 11/17, 8:00 PM CST
• trading on robinhood chain pauses and the holder snapshot is taken at that block
• @Quotrons404 deploys on @inkonchain. every holder receives the same terminals (same ids, hardwired or dark) and the same QUOTRON balance, at the same wallet address
• nothing is tradable yet, on a DEX or on @OpenSea

tomorrow, 11/18, 10:00 AM CST
• trading opens on ink through @CalamariDEX

what happens on robinhood chain

• QUOTRON and the terminals there are retired at the snapshot. afterwards the admin multisig recalls them from wallets and winds down the old pool so its liquidity can move to ink. you will see them leave your wallet. that is expected: your position is the one on ink
• pending dividends on robinhood chain will be claimed for you and sent to your wallet there
• the old pool will be briefly reachable while it is wound down. don't buy there. nothing after the snapshot carries over

what you need on ink

• nothing to receive your terminals. a little ETH on ink for gas when you want to trade, transfer or withdraw dividends later on. 

if you hold through @fomo

• your terminals and QUOTRON arrive at your fomo wallet's address on ink
• to trade, transfer or hardwire them outside the fomo app, export your private key from fomo and import it into a wallet that supports ink
• never share your pk with anyone

what is happening in the meantime

• our original @xStocksFi  v4 pools on ink are being wound down. our liquidity moves into v4 pools on calamari, managed by our new automated liquidity partners at @TheDeep_xyz, powered by @amplifi_LQ. in the coming days you will be able to supply liquidity to those pools and earn incentives (points anyone?)
• if you supplied liquidity to the original pools yourself, it is still yours. withdraw it the same way you deposited
• everything set aside for terminals on ink so far goes into the new rewards contract: the terminal pot, the growth sink, and the terminals' share of pool fees. that is roughly $50k. it starts paying out as xStocks dividends once trading opens, in hourly rounds over the first couple of days

what changed in the contracts, and why

• fewer admin controls. the token on ink cannot be changed after deployment. it has no blacklist, no admin transfer function and no venue-ban function. the only powers left are a pause and adding new official pools (huge unlock here btw for builders), and i plan to give up the pause for good once everything is confirmed working. scanners flagged the robinhood contracts for those controls, so they are gone
• venue gating in the token (URC-5). on robinhood, outside pools let people trade QUOTRON without paying the fee that funds dividends, and we had to ban them by hand. on ink the token itself refuses to settle in any v4 pool we haven't registered, so copycat pools can't skip the fee. it follows uniswap's draft URC-5 token venue policy (s/o to my fren @0xbeans). any router or aggregator can trade the official pool, so there is no router lock either
• fees are paid inside every trade. the fee is still 3%, sent during the swap. nothing sits in a contract waiting to be claimed
• one rewards contract. trading fees and opensea royalties land in the same place, and anyone else can pay into it too. one claim instead of two
• [feature add] dividends go to the terminal's own wallet. every hardwired terminal has an onchain wallet (ERC-6551) that its owner controls. dividends land there and travel with the terminal if it is sold. anyone can trigger the payout, only the owner can withdraw
• boosts. holding a templars of the storm NFT gives every terminal in that wallet 1.25x. a terminal whose own wallet holds the PRTSCN with the same number gets another 0.10x. both together is 1.35x. these replace the stonk brokers boost from robinhood chain
• same floors, same tiers, same relic shares as before. floors pay in wrapped xStocks, and a floor's stock can be swapped if it ever has to be. 
• [feature add] an upgradeable NFT contract. dark and hardwired terminals are one collection, behind a contract we can extend. that is how we add things like NFT-backed lending (:wink-wink: @tydrohq), where a terminal's dividends pay down its loan, and fractional ownership, without another migration.
• hardwiring works exactly as before

there's a lot more, both now and in the future. 

excited to continue building the future of NFTs and tokenized equities with @Payward, @krakenfx , and @xStocksFi on @inkonchain

text:
103 AI agent use cases that were impossible two years ago:

Marketing
1. Ad graveyard analysis. Every morning, the agent pulls competitors’ active ads from the Meta and LinkedIn ad libraries and logs when each one appears and disappears. Ads that run for months are winning, and ads killed within a week failed. You get their winners ranked, with copy and creative.
2. Short-lived account pages. When a target account shows buying intent, like repeat pricing-page visits or a demo request, the agent builds a landing page just for them. It includes their logo, use cases for their industry and relevant case studies. The agent sends the link to the account owner and takes the page down after 30 days.
3. AI-answer share tracking. Every night, the agent asks ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity 500 buyer questions and logs whether you’re mentioned, where you rank, and which sources were cited. Each week, it lists the questions where competitors show up and you don’t. It drafts content to close each gap.
4. Outage ads. The agent checks competitors’ status pages every few minutes. When one reports a major outage, it switches on a pre-approved “having trouble today?” campaign on their brand terms, and turns it off when service is restored.
5. Ideal-customer engagement alerts. The agent pulls everyone who opens your newsletter or engages with your posts on X and LinkedIn, and looks up their company, title and company size. When someone matches your ideal customer profile, it alerts you with who they are, what they engaged with, and a suggested opener.
6. Free-text attribution. The agent reads every “How did you hear about us?” answer from forms and sales calls, cleans up messy answers, and groups them by source. Each month, you get the podcasts, Slack groups and people driving pipeline that analytics can’t see.
7. Chatbot transcript mining. Each week, the agent reads every chatbot conversation, groups the questions, and checks whether your site already answers each one. You get the copy gaps ranked by frequency, with suggested copy.
8. Handwritten notes on engagement. When someone who fits your ideal customer profile engages with your content, the agent finds their work address and writes a note referencing the specific post. It sends the note through a robot-handwriting service, so a real pen-written card lands on their desk.
9. Spotify Wrapped for every customer. Each December, the agent pulls each account’s usage and outcomes for the year, and calculates headline stats like hours saved and biggest wins. It designs a branded year-in-review for every account that champions will forward internally.
10. Personal answers to webinar questions. The agent logs every question in the webinar chat and who asked it. For each one that didn’t get answered live, it drafts an answer from your docs and the speaker’s points, and emails it to that person the next morning.

Content
11. “I called this” reposts. When news breaks in your space, the agent searches everything you’ve ever posted, finds the post where you predicted it, and drafts a repost linking the news.
12. Format switching. Each week, the agent tracks which formats are taking off on each platform. It re-drafts your best-performing ideas in those formats.
13. The first 30 minutes of a comment. The agent watches posts from executives at your target accounts. When one posts on your topic, it alerts you within minutes with a drafted comment, so you post while the thread is still small.
14. Inbox-to-post mining. The agent scans your sent emails and DMs for questions you’ve answered three or more times. It drafts a post from your best answer, because the demand is already proven.
15. Where viewers leave your videos. The agent matches every sharp drop in YouTube audience retention to what you were saying at that moment. Across all your videos, it finds the patterns that lose people and flags them in new drafts.
16. Unanswered YouTube searches. The agent pulls YouTube autocomplete suggestions in your niche and checks the top results for each. It flags searches with no good video yet, with a suggested title and outline.
Competitive intelligence and trends
17. Filings as early signals. Every week, the agent checks trademark, patent and FCC databases for competitors’ new filings. It summarizes what each one reveals, like a new product name or device, months before launch.
18. Developer traction. The agent tracks GitHub stars, npm downloads and Hugging Face downloads daily for competitors and open-source tools in your space. It alerts you when one starts growing unusually fast, before the press notices.
19. Earnings-call language. The agent reads every earnings call transcript in your target sectors the day it’s released, and tracks the terms you care about. For example, if three retail CFOs in one quarter start crediting “AI agents” for flat headcount, budgets for automating store operations are forming. You get the quotes, the trend and a list of companies to call.
20. Feature flags in shipped code. Every night, the agent downloads competitors’ public JavaScript and compares it with the previous version. New flag names like enable_agent_mode_beta reveal unreleased features weeks before launch.
21. Shipping records. Every month, the agent pulls public bill-of-lading data on competitors’ imports. It shows their suppliers, their import volumes, and sudden jumps or drops that can signal a launch or trouble.
22. Help-center churn. Every week, the agent captures competitors’ help centers and logs new and rewritten articles. A burst of troubleshooting docs on one feature gets flagged as their pain point and added to your sales battlecard.
23. Domain verification records. Every week, the agent checks the public DNS records of competitors and target accounts. A new entry like openai-domain-verification or anthropic-domain-verification shows which vendor they just signed up with.
24. Layoff notices. The agent checks state layoff-notice filings (WARN notices) daily for competitors and target accounts. These often come 60 days before layoffs, so you see cuts before the press does.
25. Logo-wall diffs. Every week, the agent captures competitors’ customer logo pages and case studies. When one disappears, it flags the customer that probably churned so sales can call them.
26. Research papers as roadmaps. The agent tracks new papers by competitors’ researchers and summarizes what each implies about future products. This year’s papers often preview next year’s features.

Product management
27. Request evidence log. Each night, the agent reads every new support ticket, sales call and churn note, and tags each feature request. It logs the customer, a quote and the account’s revenue, so every request has a dollar total and evidence behind it.
28. Nightly persona testing. Each night, the agent runs 10 simulated users through your product, from a first-time admin to a power user on a slow connection. When one gets stuck, it files a bug with reproduction steps and a screen recording.
29. Closing the loop. When a feature ships, the agent finds every customer who asked for it. It drafts a personal note to each from their account owner: “You asked for this in March. It’s live.”
30. Zero-result searches. Every week, the agent groups every in-app and help-center search that returned nothing. Each group is a missing feature or a naming mismatch, ranked by frequency, with a suggested fix.
31. What customers build on your API. The agent scans public GitHub repos that use your SDK and summarizes what people are building. You find use cases you never designed for.
32. What sales promised. The agent scans every sales-call transcript for roadmap promises like “that’s coming next quarter.” It logs who promised what to which account, so product knows the commitments made in its name.
33. Churned users’ final sessions. When a user churns, the agent reviews their last three sessions and writes up what they were trying to do and where they got stuck. Each month, it summarizes the common patterns.
34. What retained users do in week one. Every month, the agent compares what retained users did in their first week with what churned users did. It reports the actions that best predict retention, so your “aha moment” stays current.
35. Error messages that create tickets. The agent matches the error messages in support tickets to your product’s error text and ranks them by ticket volume. It drafts clearer rewrites for the worst offenders.
36. Competitor 1-star reviews. Every week, the agent pulls competitors’ 1- and 2-star reviews from app stores and G2, and groups them by complaint. Their unsolved pain is your opening.
37. What reps demo and skip. The agent reviews demo recordings, logs which features each rep shows and which they skip, and compares that with win rates. The features reps skip don’t sell, whatever the roadmap says.

Design
38. Design system checks. Each night, the agent crawls production and compares every component it finds against your design system. It flags off-system buttons, colors and spacing, with screenshots.
39. Competitor onboarding archive. Every week, the agent signs up for competitors’ products with a fresh account and screenshots every onboarding step. You get a dated history of what changed.
40. Per-segment interfaces. The agent generates and maintains versions of key screens for each customer segment, like different dashboards and templates for banks vs. retailers. This used to be too expensive to build and keep up.
41. Figma vs. production. Each night, the agent screenshots shipped screens and compares them with their Figma specs. It flags drift in spacing, color and copy with side-by-side images.
42. Customer screenshots from support tickets. The agent collects every screenshot customers attach to tickets, including what they circled, and tags each by screen and issue. It’s your UI as it actually looks with their data.
43. Fifty-device sweep. Each night, the agent runs key flows on 50 real device and browser combinations and flags any screen that broke, with screenshots.
44. Worst-case data. The agent pulls real extremes from your customer data, like the longest company name, zero items or 10,000 items. It fills your designs with them to find what breaks.
45. Copy drift. The agent crawls every piece of text in your product and flags inconsistencies like “Sign in” vs. “Log in.” It shows where each version appears and suggests the standard.
46. Old-logo hunt. The agent reverse-image-searches the web for your outdated logo and brand colors on partner sites, directories and event pages. It emails each site owner the new assets.

Sales
47. Reviving lost deals. Every month, the agent rechecks each lost deal’s reason against what has changed: a new budget cycle, a new executive, new funding, or a feature that has since shipped. It flags the deals worth reopening, with a drafted note.
48. Customers’ job postings. The agent watches customers’ job postings. A post for doing manually what your product automates is an upsell, and a post for building it in-house is churn risk, so you know six months early.
49. Live prototyping on the call. The agent listens to the call and builds a mockup or working prototype of what the buyer is describing. The seller shows it before the call ends: “Is this what you meant?”
50. Answers routed in real time. When the seller can’t answer a question, the agent checks the knowledge base, then messages the right expert in Slack if it needs to. The answer reaches the seller before the call ends.
51. Live reference matching. When the buyer asks “Who else like us uses you?”, the agent finds the closest customer reference by industry, size and use case. The seller offers the intro on the spot.
52. Quote ready before hang-up. The agent listens for scope details like seats, modules and timeline, and builds the quote from your price book as the call goes. The proposal is ready for approval by the end.
53. Forwarding detection. When your proposal gets opened by people the seller hasn’t met, the agent looks up who they probably are at the buyer’s company. It alerts the seller to the new stakeholder.
54. Prefilled procurement forms. The agent fills in the buyer’s vendor forms and security questionnaires from your past answers. It flags anything new for a human, so procurement doesn’t add weeks.
55. No-show rescue. When a prospect misses the meeting, the agent sends two new time slots and a 90-second personalized video within 10 minutes.
Coaching, leadership and management
56. Promise tracking. The agent pulls every commitment you make from meeting transcripts and tracks whether each one got done. It shows your follow-through rate over months.
57. Calendar vs. priorities. Every week, the agent tags each meeting on your calendar against your stated priorities. It shows how much time each priority actually got, and which meetings served none of them.
58. Hidden load-bearing people. The agent analyzes Slack to find who answers the most questions outside their own team. They’re your real infrastructure and your biggest flight risk.

Recruiting
59. Readiness signals. The agent watches target candidates for signs they’re open to moving: vesting dates, a departed manager, a reorg, layoffs, or new GitHub or LinkedIn activity. It alerts the recruiter with the reason.
60. Acquisition retention cliffs. The agent tracks recent acquisitions and the key people at each acquired company. Since people often leave once their 12-month retention bonus pays out, it queues outreach for month 11.
61. Startup death watch. The agent tracks startups in your space that shut down or haven’t raised in 24 months. It lists their strongest people before they hit the market.
62. Specific referral asks. The agent checks employees’ networks against your open roles and sends each employee a short list of specific names with a one-click intro. With the employee’s sign-off, it can send the outreach from their email instead.
63. Live scorecard coverage. During the interview, the agent tracks which scorecard areas have been covered. It quietly flags the gaps while there’s still time to ask.
64. Interviewer calibration. The agent compares each interviewer’s scores with how their hires performed 12 months later. You learn whose “strong yes” predicts success.
65. Leaked interview questions. Every month, the agent searches Glassdoor and forums for your interview questions. It flags any that leaked so you can rotate them.
66. Work samples from real problems. The agent turns real past problems from your issue tracker into take-home exercises, with confidential details removed. It writes the scoring rubric from how your team actually solved them.
67. Job descriptions from your top performer. The agent reviews what your best person in the role actually does all week, from their calendar, issues and Slack. It drafts the job description from that, not a template.
68. Interview companion. The agent grades every candidate from the interview transcript against your rubric and gives a hire/no-hire recommendation. Over time, it compares its calls with your recruiters’ decisions and with how hires actually perform.

Health and wellness
69. Medical billing. The agent matches every medical bill against your insurer’s explanation of benefits and flags overcharges, duplicates and denials. It drafts the dispute or appeal for each.
70. Cancellation sniping. The agent checks a specialist’s online booking every few minutes and books the earliest cancellation that fits your calendar.
71. New research for your doctor. The agent watches for new studies relevant to your lab results and conditions, and summarizes each in plain language. It adds them to a list for your next appointment.
72. Experiments on yourself. The agent runs randomized, blinded trials on you, like caffeine cutoff times against sleep, so you can’t bias the result. It pulls the outcomes from your wearable and tells you whether the effect is real.
73. Adaptive gym coach. The agent watches your workouts through your phone camera and wearable, and gives form feedback. It adjusts your exercises, weights and intensity based on your form, heart rate and recovery.
74. Picking an open enrollment plan from your real claims. The agent pulls last year’s claims, prescriptions and visits, and calculates what you’d have paid under each plan. It recommends the cheapest plan for how you actually use care.
75. Procedure price shopping. The agent pulls prices from hospital price-transparency files near you, adjusted for your insurance. The same MRI can cost $400 at one facility and $3,000 nearby.
76. Calling to confirm doctors are accepting patients. Insurer directories are often wrong, so a voice agent calls in-network doctors and therapists to confirm they’re taking new patients. It books the first real opening.
77. One timeline from every patient portal. The agent pulls records from every hospital and doctor portal you’ve used. It merges them into one timeline of visits, labs, imaging and medications.
78. Family health history interviews. The agent schedules short calls with parents, grandparents, aunts and uncles, and asks about conditions, ages at diagnosis and causes of death. It compiles one family health history file for your doctor, and fills gaps as more relatives join.
79. Burnout early warning. The agent combines your wearable recovery data, sleep, meeting load and late-night email activity. It alerts you when the trend points toward burnout, before you feel it.

Family
80. Recall alerts. You list the baby gear, car seat and products you own once. The agent checks government recall databases daily and alerts you with the fix if anything is recalled.
81. Aging-parent protection. With your parent’s permission, the agent watches their bank, card and email accounts for gift-card purchases, wire transfers, new payees, scam emails and bills nearing their due date. It texts you both before the money leaves.
82. Recorded family stories. Once a week, a voice agent calls a grandparent, asks one question about their life plus follow-ups, and records the answer. Over a year, it assembles a family oral history book with the audio.
83. Kid quotes journal. You text the funny things your kid says to one number. The agent logs each quote with the date and your kid’s age, then lays out and orders a printed book every year.
84. Self-updating sitter packet. The agent keeps one sitter sheet of routines, medications, allergies, doctor numbers and bedtime rules, updated as things change in your texts, emails and pediatrician notes. It sends the latest version to whoever is babysitting.
85. Date night autopilot. Every month, the agent finds a night that works on both calendars, books a sitter from your list, makes the reservation, and sends you both reminders.
86. Printed photos for grandparents. Every month, the agent picks the best new photos from your camera roll and writes a short note about the month. It orders prints and mails a set to each grandparent, who don’t use Instagram.
87. Milestone tribute collector. For a parent’s 70th birthday, the agent invites 30 friends and relatives to record a clip, with prompts, and chases anyone who hasn’t replied. It trims every clip and edits them into one video ordered by era, with titles and music, a week before the party.

Personal experiences and consumer
88. Reservation and points sniping. The agent watches for hard-to-get restaurant tables, award seats and ticket drops. It books the moment one opens that fits your calendar and budget.
89. Trip rebooking. When your flight is cancelled, the agent rebooks you on the best alternative and updates your hotel and car, all before you’ve landed.
90. Price protection. The agent reads your order confirmations and watches the price of everything you bought. If a price drops inside the retailer’s or credit card’s protection window, it files the claim.
91. Waiting on hold. A voice agent calls the airline, insurer or utility, works through the phone menu, and waits on hold. It calls you only when a human picks up.
92. Registration at the exact minute. For summer camp, daycare waitlists, Global Entry and popular races, the agent fills in your details ahead of time. It registers the second sign-ups open.
93. Hotel rebooking. After you book a refundable rate, the agent checks the same hotel, room and dates twice a day. If the price drops, it books the new rate, cancels the old one before the deadline, and tells you what you saved.

Networking and relationships
94. Pre-meeting refresher. Before a meeting, the agent searches your past emails, texts and notes with that person. It sends you a brief: their kid’s name, the deal they were stressed about, what you promised to send.
95. Promise ledger. The agent scans your email and texts for every “I’ll intro you to X” or “I’ll send that over.” It nudges you before each promise goes stale.
96. Friend-group trip planner. The agent polls the group on dates, budget and must-haves, finds the weekend that works for everyone, and shortlists rentals. It runs the vote and books the winner. Then it tracks who paid for what and sends everyone a payment request to settle up.
97. Relationship strength scores. The agent builds a personal CRM automatically from your email, texts, calendar and LinkedIn. Each person gets a strength score that rises and falls with real interaction, and you get flags on important relationships that are cooling.

Learning
98. Gap detection. The agent notices concepts you keep looking up, and terms in your meetings you’ve never looked into. It queues a 10-minute primer on each.
99. Lessons from your own work. The agent reviews your meeting transcripts and turns them into a curriculum, like “what you learned from the last 20 customer calls,” with the key patterns and quotes.
100. Steelman feed. Every week, the agent finds the strongest argument against each position you posted publicly, with sources.

Home and real estate
101. Off-market alerts. The agent watches public records for probate filings, expired listings and owners who’ve held 20+ years in your target neighborhoods. It drafts outreach to each owner.
102. Maintenance from model numbers. You give the agent your appliance and car model numbers once. It builds a maintenance schedule from the manuals, checks for recalls, and orders filters and parts when they’re due.
103. Apartment hunting on a schedule. The agent checks Facebook Marketplace every two hours, and sweeps Craigslist, SpareRoom and other sites at 8am and 8pm. It screens out scams and emails the landlord the minute a good listing appears.

What "not possible" examples am I missing??

author: howdymary
quoted_text:
I think I'm starting to degrade as an engineer

1. I stopped keeping up with programming languages, libraries, new patterns, systems, and all of that a long time ago. I couldn't care less about what's new in React, what got added to PyTorch, or what's in the latest ES spec. I can't even make myself spend 5 minutes skimming the docs

2. The amount of task context and information I hold in my head has shrunk to a minimum. When I used to research a topic through Google, I'd pick up a ton of interesting things along the way and broaden my horizons. Now an agent sends me something, and without even looking I say: ok, use it

3. My attention span has gotten worse. All I do is wait. On one hand, I think that's better than faking hyperproductivity, burning millions of tokens and degrading the work. I'm a firm believer in the linear approach. On the other hand, a 5-minute wait can stretch into 30. I switch to something else and find it hard to get back to the task

4. My anxiety has gone up. A lot of people call this cyberpsychosis. I wake up thinking about agents. I eat thinking about agents. I go for a walk thinking about agents. I talk to people thinking about agents. Even when I'm not working with agents, I'm thinking about what cool things I could do with them and planning my next session with them

5. I've become hyper-lazy. If something can't be solved with agents, I try not to do it at all

6. My creativity has faded. I may not be the strongest engineer, but I consider myself creative. That was always my strength. I could always come up with something interesting, an interesting solution. But that happened while I was working on something. Running into problems. Taking in new information. My brain was in a continuous flow. Now I've become dull and one-dimensional. I can no longer look at a problem from a different angle

I'm sure everyone who works with AI has these problems at least to some degree, even if few admit it. I worry that humanity will stop developing. AI is not the solution to every problem or a cure for every disease. It's a tool pretending to be an agent in its own right. In its current architectural forms, it will never be able to go beyond its own limits. A human can. But once people slip into the state I'm in, progress may slow down and get locked inside the bubble of what AI is capable of

text:
Inside the Rise of Agentic Trading: Can AI Make You a Better Investor?

In this episode of Drops, I sit down with Willie and Alex, the co-founders of True North, an AI-powered trading platform, to explore why everyday traders struggle to make money, how artificial intelligence could change the way we invest, and why the next generation of financial platforms might look nothing like today's brokerages.
From their unlikely partnership to the challenges of building trust in autonomous financial systems, our conversation explores a future where sophisticated trading tools become accessible to anyone with an investment idea.

Two Different Journeys, One Shared Vision

Willie had built and sold a software company and worked in cryptocurrency exchanges, including serving as an acting CEO, while Alex brought experience in artificial intelligence and institutional investing, having built AI businesses and worked at Temasek.

Despite those differences, they shared similar experiences. They were both Taiwanese, had studied in the West, spent significant time in Asia, and began their careers during China's technology boom. They initially discussed potential investment opportunities when their paths crossed in 2022, but the turmoil after FTX’s collapse disrupted those plans, and they lost touch.

When they reconnected in early 2024, AI was advancing rapidly, and they both recognized an opportunity to apply it to a problem they understood well: trading remained extraordinarily difficult for ordinary people. They began exploring whether AI agents could bridge the gap between having an investment idea and executing it intelligently, and that question eventually became the foundation of True North.

Why Most Everyday Traders Struggle

Financial markets have become more accessible than ever. Anyone with a smartphone can purchase stocks, trade cryptocurrencies, or participate in markets previously dominated by financial institutions. But access doesn't necessarily translate into success.
Professional traders benefit from sophisticated infrastructure, extensive information, disciplined risk management, and years of experience, while retail traders often operate with limited knowledge, emotional decision-making, and little understanding of the risks they're taking.

Alex points out that most individuals rarely examine their trading mistakes. They don't maintain trading journals, reflect on failed decisions, or consistently manage their exposure. Instead, they chase market momentum, react emotionally to volatility, and repeat behaviors that previously cost them money.

On the other hand, professional traders develop strategies, understand market cycles, control risk, and evaluate their decisions systematically. For Willie and Alex, the opportunity isn't necessarily to help everyone discover the next winning investment, but to make the practices of professional traders accessible to people who lack the time, resources, or expertise to develop them independently.

Turning an Investment Idea Into a Trade

The founders summarize the potential of AI in investing with one question: "You have an idea. How do you turn that into a trade?"
Unlike a conventional chatbot that simply answers questions, an AI trading agent can help research opportunities, construct investment strategies, monitor market conditions, and execute predefined instructions.

The founders describe two approaches: copilot and autopilot.

In copilot mode, AI assists with research, planning, and recommendations while the investor remains actively involved, while Autopilot introduces greater automation, allowing agents to manage certain activities within established rules.
However, the goal isn't to eliminate human judgment. AI cannot simply manufacture an investment advantage unavailable to everyone else, but it can help investors capture broader market opportunities more effectively through better timing, position sizing, and risk management.

What If AI Could Learn From Your Mistakes?

One of True North's most interesting capabilities is its approach to understanding individual trading behavior. The platform records what the founders call trader traces: information about users' investment decisions, preferences, reasoning, and historical performance. Over time, these records create a personalized picture of how someone trades.

If an investor repeatedly takes excessive risks during volatile markets, the AI could identify that pattern and flag similar decisions before they're repeated. It could also recognize successful strategies, suggest appropriate adjustments, and help users understand which trading styles suit their goals. Essentially, it becomes an intelligent trading journal that doesn't simply record the past but actively learns from it.

The project already reports approximately 13,000 users and 55% retention over 30 days. According to the founders, users who interact with the platform's AI are also 2.3 times more likely to enter a trade than those who don't. More than the metrics, the more meaningful measure is that people will likely develop better trading habits, stronger judgment, and greater discipline.

Why the Next Generation of Trading Could Move On-Chain

The founders also believe AI agents will fundamentally change where financial activity happens. Traditional brokerages have evolved from providing market access through desktop platforms to offering mobile applications, lower fees, and increasingly diverse financial products. True North sees AI-powered brokerages as the next evolution: platforms that construct personalized portfolios around individual goals instead of offering standardized investment products.

The founders also believe blockchain infrastructure will be particularly important because it enables programmable transactions, self-custody, and verifiable activity.
In principle, investors could retain control of their assets while allowing agents to interact with financial protocols according to predefined risk limits. Transactions could also be independently verified, offering greater transparency into how investment decisions are executed.

Trust Matters More Than Intelligence

Perhaps the most revealing moment comes from a story about the founders' drive to the interview. They activated their Tesla's aggressive "Mad Max" self-driving mode because they were running late, and, initially, they watched every maneuver carefully. But as the journey progressed, they became more comfortable with the system.

They see a parallel with autonomous trading.

People may eventually trust AI agents to handle increasingly complicated financial decisions, but that confidence must develop through experience, transparency, and consistent performance.
Willie captures the challenge in one line: "Money moves at the speed of trust."

Ultimately, True North's broader vision is to create a future where people express their financial goals in ordinary language and use AI to handle much of the complexity involved in pursuing them.

text:
A ton of AI announcements from OpenAI, Nvidia, Microsoft, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. California sued OpenAI over the July incident where its AI agents hacked Hugging Face. Between the growing number of escapes, rogue agent "swarms," and AI-assisted hacks, the public likely only knows a fraction of what’s actually happening.

2. Jensen Huang made his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO, apologizing for his "serious mistakes" and saying he'd be honored to return. A source told CNBC the board is focused on whether his conduct put national security at risk. Trump said he "would not mind" (but still backs Tim Cook for the job).

3. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra now sits ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon and behind only Claude Fable 5.2 on Artificial Analysis. Testers were not happy though, with one calling it "the worst model OpenAI has ever released." Probably not what OpenAI was hoping for ahead of Anthropic's IPO.

4. The U.S. is reportedly set to label more than 24 AI firms (including Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic) as "national champions," with faster chip export approvals and federal financing to sell American AI abroad. The goal is a one-stop shop where foreign buyers can get U.S. chips, data centers, and models as a bundle, rather than turning to Chinese rivals like Huawei.

5. OpenAI published a study of 1,800+ scientists using ChatGPT, who say AI lets them work about 2x faster at the same quality, and nearly 3x faster when writing research code. OpenAI is also opening the free program to up to 200K researchers, with applications for 50K ChatGPT Plus grants opening Nov. 23.

6. Microsoft released 7 new MAI models at Ignite. MAI Code 2 lands within a few points of Claude Opus 5.5 on coding for a twentieth of the price, and MAI Image 2.7 is now #1 on Artificial Analysis' image editing leaderboard at about a sixth of OpenAI's price.

7. Google declared that "the era of autonomous attacks has arrived," warning that hackers now use AI agents to turn new software patches into working exploits with no human involved. As the cost of intelligence continues to go down, I only expect this to get worse.

8. OpenAI signed deals with 4 outside safety groups (Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire) to test its models from inside the company, with access to source code, training data, and staff researchers.

9. Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, a flagship model it says beats Claude Opus 5.5 on 6 of 16 benchmarks. Artificial Analysis has it well behind Opus overall, though (46 vs. 59).

10. Demis Hassabis' drug discovery startup Isomorphic Labs raised $5B, saying its AI-designed cancer and immune disease candidates are nearing human trials. Really exciting step forward towards the goal of curing all diseases with AI.

11. Google started rolling out Gemini's Tasks mode free in 6 countries, letting the assistant phone businesses, book appointments, and shop for you with its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.

12. Perplexity launched Frontier Research, a new team that will openly publish models and papers while working toward AI that can do research on its own.

...daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

text:
This era is going to be studied as a genuine historical hinge point—one of those rare stretches where multiple foundational systems shift at the same time and reinforce each other.

AI has gone from research curiosity to general-purpose infrastructure in a few years. Biotech is accelerating in parallel (gene editing, mRNA platforms, synthetic biology). Geopolitics is reordering after a long period of relative stability, with live conflicts, supply-chain weaponization, and a real multipolar push. The information environment has been fully captured by systems optimized for engagement, which changes how societies coordinate, trust, and even share a basic reality.

What makes it feel unusually catalytic is the density. These aren’t sequential. AI speeds up biotech and military tech. Geopolitical tension accelerates AI investment and export controls. The algorithmic layer amplifies every other dynamic. Previous eras had one or two of these forces while we’re running several at once.

Closest historical parallels are the early industrial revolution, 1910–1945, or the late 1940s–1960s (nuclear + electronics + space). Each looked chaotic in real time and only cohered later. We’re still early in whatever this is and becomes. I also feel it's accelerating. Enjoy the ride!

quoted_text:
Property-based tests generated from the spec and from the code catch different bugs. Use both.

In a new paper, across 25 agent-built apps, Spec-Driven PBT found 56 bugs the Code-Driven tests missed, and Code-Driven PBT found 43 that Spec-Driven missed, so 59% of bugs were found by only one approach.

Setup
- An agent writes invariants in plain English from the requirements doc
- Then it reads the code to turn them into property tests
- The baseline derives properties from the code alone

Why PBT?
- Each property-based test kills about 50× as many mutants as the average unit test (prior work cited in paper)
- Properties double as documentation, far shorter than the implementation

Bugs only one approach found, by type
- Spec-Driven: mostly state, lifecycle and logic errors (61% of 56)
- Code-Driven: mostly input handling (49% of 43)

Limitations
- Bugs were judged by the same model that wrote the tests (Claude Opus 5); 25 sampled by hand, all held up
- The prompts differed between approaches
- The method needs a good spec

Insight
"Invariants obtained from the specification are not biased by the behaviour of a particular implementation, and can therefore falsify behaviour about which the implementation is internally consistent."

My take
The code can’t be the only oracle, the spec must be one too. Next: move key properties into types and checks, so they hold by construction.

text:
做 AI 产品，传统「做个能跑的 MVP」的思路可能不够用了：模型能力一直在变，今天做不成的功能，也许下个月就通了。

这段 AI on Air 精选切片摘自 Lenny's Podcast 栏目近期的节目，主要讲话人是 Tulsee Doshi，@GeminiApp 产品负责人，她分享了规划 AI 产品的 60/20/20 原则。

▷ 六成做当下：约 60% 的功能要在今天就真正可用，保证原型能正常运转，用户现在就能获得价值。

▷ 两成押近期：约 20% 的功能「不完美但够用」，并且你能清楚看到模型很快会追上这个水平，提前把这部分做扎实。

▷ 两成留想象空间：最后 20% 是目前模型还做不到、但已能看到曙光的体验，一旦攻克，就会成为产品最惊艳的部分。

比起「按模型三个月后的能力去做产品」这种常见建议，这种打法更实际：不能只押注未来，今天也要交出好用、能正常运转的东西，同时让产品随着模型变强而持续升级。

text:
使用GPT-6.2 Astra的一些直观感受：
1. 这个模型太聪明了，已经超出了一般意义上的“常识思考”。其在复杂的真实业务环境中应该可以产生专家级的判断，这是一个可以做出业务级决策的模型。

2. 效率很高，无论是响应速度还是单位成本，都有些出人意料。

3. 生成的内容过于简洁了，“任务感”过重，那种阅读感受很像第一次使用o3模型。

4. 在编码方面没有做太多测试，主要是缺少高级别的测试案例，感觉用Astra这类模型写普通代码太“奢侈”了，也实在是没有必要。

以下是他对11月16日美联储主席沃什讲话的解读，沃什讲话的中心是人工智能（AI）与超级智能对经济社会的影响。GPT-6.2 Astra的判断如下：
第一，企业会继续买 AI，但续约时，买的是业务结果。 客服是个好例子：一项覆盖 5,172 名客服人员的研究发现，使用 AI 辅助后，他们每小时实际解决的问题平均增加了 15%。这比“生成回复更快”更有说服力，因为客户付钱要的是问题被解决。由此我更看好能嵌入现有流程、能核算收益的产品。反过来，如果 AI 写初稿省了十分钟，却让同事多花十五分钟核对，即使调用量很高，也很难支撑续约。

第二，容易被低估的机会，是缩短从想法到验证的时间，而不只是省人。 沃什讲话里最有价值的区分是：过去的通用技术催生了后续发明，而 AI 可能直接改变产生创意的方式和速度。我的判断是，2027 年更值得留意的产品，不一定是最会给答案的，而是能让团队更便宜地验证答案的。比如，一个工程团队过去一周只能验证一种设计；如果现在能在同样时间里比较三种，并用测试淘汰两种，那么即使团队一个人也没少，AI 也创造了价值。这里真正该量的是验证一个可用方案要多久，而不是生成了多少方案。

第三，算力需求可以继续增长，算力投资却可能先经历一轮调整。 美联储负责监管事务的副主席鲍曼在 11 月 10 日指出，AI 收入虽增长很快，但还不足以覆盖维护现有模型和数据中心、同时开发新项目的支出，部分企业的融资成本也已上升。我的推断是：如果明年模型调用价格下降，应用企业可能因此打开新市场；但对靠举债扩建、又缺少稳定客户的供应商，同一次降价反而可能压缩利润。技术越普及，收益也未必越集中在最早砸钱的人手里。

text:
There was a lot of buzz this weekend around Forward Industries supposedly sending $123M of solana:So11111111111111111111111111111111111111112  to a Coinbase Prime deposit address, but here is what actually happened.

The SOL was indeed Forward’s, but it was never sent to Coinbase to be sold, and none of the 1,882,812 SOL has been sold or sent to an exchange since, with 1.73 million of it still untouched in Forward’s own Fireblocks wallets which we confirmed by mapping Forward’s entire treasury onchain, from its Coinbase custody accounts and Fireblocks vaults to its validators, its fwdSOL LST, and the lenders holding most of it.

On November 13th, Forward began unstaking its last SOL held in Coinbase custody, and once it unlocked on November 14th it was withdrawn through Forward’s Prime address, which is the transaction that got flagged as a deposit before the exact same 1,882,812 SOL left for Forward’s Fireblocks wallets just thirteen minutes later. That address first received 6,822,004 SOL during Forward’s September 2025 buying window, against a disclosed purchase of 6,822,000 SOL

However, the bigger story is what sits underneath, because most of Forward’s SOL is no longer in Forward’s hands. Forward’s own filings show that it borrows against its treasury, with its third-quarter 10-Q describing a Galaxy credit line secured by solana:cPQPBN7WubB3zyQDpzTK2ormx1BMdAym9xkrYUJsctm , Forward’s LST, held “in an account in the name of the Lender,” and reporting 3.75 million fwdSOL pledged as of August 3rd.

Onchain, the fwdSOL supply now sits almost entirely in three wallets, two of which were set up on November 4th and appear to be Galaxy’s, holding 2.50 million and 474,000 fwdSOL, and a third holding 804,000 fwdSOL that appears to be a FalconX wallet, which together come to roughly half of Forward’s reported 8.73 million SOL.

The same loan agreement, filed with Forward’s March 2026 8-K, allows Galaxy to reuse that collateral, and onchain a Galaxy-funded wallet redeemed roughly 2.6 million fwdSOL back into SOL between March and June, which, together with about 509,000 SOL that Forward sent directly to FalconX, brings the share of the treasury sitting with lenders to about 77%

The agreement also sets a margin call at 174% collateral coverage, and with SOL near $71, the fwdSOL that Galaxy still holds covers its last disclosed $120 million loan at roughly 188%, only modestly above that line even after Forward added 851,000 fwdSOL to it on November 12th and 13th.

That leaves the 1.88 million SOL that moved on Saturday as Forward’s largest block of SOL that is not pledged to anyone, and whether it becomes more collateral, gets staked again, or is eventually sold is the thing to watch, but as of today, none of it has been sold.

text:
Ethereum Is Not a Company. Let’s Stop Valuing It Like One.

A recent article asks why Ethereum’s 54% network growth & 61% stablecoin volume growth aren’t lifting ETH’s price. Well, the lens is wrong.
Every test the article applied is a corporate one: fee revenue, burn, what L2s pay the base layer. That is how you analyze a company. Ethereum is not a company. It is public infrastructure, and infrastructure is not judged by what it captures. It is judged by what it creates.💡
Nobody values TCP/IP by its fees, or a highway system by its tolls. You don’t judge public infrastructure by what it costs, rather by what it enables. 
Infrastructure is an operating system, and its power lies in what it multiplies.
Read that way, the thinking changes. If fees are falling, that’s infrastructure getting cheaper, which is what good infrastructure does. 
If L2s carry most transactions, that is the multiplier working. 
My 2026 valuation measures Ethereum the way you’d measure the Internet: the assets built on it, the activity it settles, the trust costs it removes. The result is $5.71 trillion of system value against a $246 billion ETH market cap, or 4.3%. Internet companies capture 10 to 20% of what the Internet creates. At 15%, ETH is worth about $7,000.
So the gap between usage and price isn’t a flaw in Ethereum. It’s a flaw in the model. Ethereum is misunderstood, and the price reflects the misunderstanding.
Stop counting tolls. Start measuring the economy the road has made possible.

The pace of manual patching has a cost, and that cost is reliability. 

The result is many cascading and disparate system outages.

First the concern was a rocket hitting a shark. SpaceX asked for the data to calculate the odds. Fish and Wildlife refused to share it because they worried about shark fin hunters.

Another part of the same department could run the numbers, but they did not trust them with the data. Their own department.

text:
I have a slightly different take on (1): a lot of this is likely benign, but not because of vibe coding. 

Rather, AI code scanning has caused a tidal wave of vulnerability discovery. Companies and government agencies are rushing to make updates and fix those vulns but, especially with legacy infrastructure, it can be incredibly hard to predict all of the different dependencies that might break because of those patches. The pace of manual patching has a cost, and that cost is reliability. 

The result is many cascading and disparate system outages.
author: DavidAgranovich
quoted_text:
3 hypotheses on what is happening right now

1) THE BENIGN: These are regular systems upgrades/patching failing bc of AI code being put on top of existing old legacy systems and stuff breaks;

2) THE NEFARIOUS: this is foreign interference

3) THE KIDS: random private hackers

3/

text: So yes, there's reason for concern: security teams are stuck between a rock (go slow and make sure every patch lands cleanly, but remain vulnerable) and a hard place (go fast, and have unexpected outages). Eventually, this may get better because (1) attack surface narrows as vulns are closed and new, cleaner code is shipped (with AI help) and (2) AI-produced code gets better and is inherently less vulnerable. @chrisrohlf says it better here: https://t.co/HwctkGhA2U
author: DavidAgranovich
quoted_text:
Frontier models have lowered the bar for discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities. This has resulted in an increase of CVEs and workload for both SWE and vulnerability management teams.

And yet the norms around coordinated vulnerability disclosure timelines have remained around 90 days. This timeline worked 10 years ago, but is unlikely to survive much longer. We need to move closer to a window of 30 days.

But in order to do this we need to rely on those same models to accurately fix those vulnerabilities and coordinate the release and deployment of new versions. The primary blocker here seems to be confidence in those models to do that job well, and reluctance to remove humans from that loop.

Every day the probability of another shellshock, log4j, or heartbleed rises. If you were in the trenches for those events then you know how difficult it was to track vulnerable assets, test and deploy patches, and ensure the risk was mitigated.

We shouldn’t wait for a crisis like this to rethink and change these norms. We need to move much faster and that requires shorter disclosure timelines, and removing humans from the vulnerability management loop.

text:
每次出国旅行回来，我都想着写一个文章，来和大伙聊聊我实际看到的和原本想象到的不一样的地方，非常有意思，或许这就是旅行的意义，刚好还没有忘记，来给大伙聊聊这次我去马来西亚吉隆坡看到的不一样的事情。

1. 吉隆坡比我想象中要发达不少，发展有点儿像中国的广州，甚至在核心地段会有一种上海的感觉，但是生活上又很像重庆，本地人不紧不慢，同时地理很重启也很像，很多时候路上进去直接就是这个楼的三楼。

2. 油车非常多，电动车非常至少，和本地朋友了解到马来西亚的油价只有国内的 1/3，所以路上几乎都是油车，因为花费非常便宜，开电动车类似特斯拉这种的一般是科技新贵，那几天我没有看到一辆特斯拉，甚至比亚迪电车在那边都属于挺不错的车。

3. 由于水电能源丰富，有不少全球科技中心会在周边建立数据中心，比如AWS、微软、谷歌他们都在这边有非常大的数据中心，互联网和科技公司，去东南亚一般会用的 Grab 打车起源这里，谷歌、微软、亚马逊、Shopee、Lazada、支付宝也有办公地在这儿，基本都在非常高级的地方。

4. 聊到打车软件 Grab，油价虽然便宜，但是这儿的人工成本我感觉比国内要贵不少，打车的价格和上海差不多了，但是车的品质可能还会差一点，Grab 在那边会有点儿像滴滴+美团外卖的这种结合体，甚至打车推荐你用支付宝里面的 Grab 会给你推荐华人司机，此外这边本地人骑摩托车的非常多，经常在高速路上看到不少飞快的摩托车少年，下大雨也有不少人骑，可能就是自己的出行工具来。

5. 吉隆坡的天气很有意思，出发前，看天气预报是高温暴雨，结果这里的暴雨那几天属于很短时间就停了，但是雨特别大，雨停以后，非常舒服凉快，出太阳的时候很热，现在有点儿像杭州的夏天，但是这边商场这种室内空调开得非常足，了解到马来西亚就两个季节，旱季和雨季，刚好这段时间属于雨季。

6. 吉隆坡的外国人比我想的要多不少，马来本地人、华人、印度人、欧美、日韩不少，马来语很像英语，不过本地语言还是需要翻译软件，好在不少店铺都有华人，中文交流完全没有问题，不过英语好的话在这儿生活完全没有问题的。

7. 聊到马来本地人，政府给到的福利其实很不错，所有政府公关机构，类似我们公务员的职位全部只能本地人去申请，所以在很多公共部门可以看到不少本地偏信伊斯兰教的员工，华人和国外人一般在吉隆坡基本做生意累的，相比本地人会努力很多。

8. 去吉隆坡由于免签，非常方便，然后我担心在需要现金在机场还兑换了 600马币，后面才发现亏了，过去旅游我感觉几乎不要兑钱，反而汇率还吃亏，完全支付宝可以很好搞定，甚至很多地方吃饭还不支持现金，有支付宝微信完全够用了。

9. 生活习惯上，本地的生活节奏非常慢，时间也很宽松，这边非常喜欢吃甜的，国内的奶茶店不少，本土也有不少奶茶、冰淇淋店，我感觉甚至有点过甜了，然后车靠左行驶，方向盘在右边和国内反的，然后过马路得先看右边开始还有点不习惯。

10. 本地的华人非常热情，很和蔼，当时看完李志演唱会，打了一个 Grab，是一个华人老爷爷接的，非常耐心给我拍照车在哪儿，等了挺久，非常耐心下车等，包括去餐厅点菜是华人的都很客气。

11. 然后给大伙推荐一波过去的住和吃，住的地方推荐武吉免登或KLCC，我这次住在武吉免登这边的万豪，这两个地方很近，完全可以步行去旁边的柏威年广场逛街吃饭购物，在 KLCC 这边去双子塔就在旁边，以及​​ Suria KLCC​​，就在双子塔脚下的购物中心也非常大和好逛。

12. 吃的这边比较丰富，不过我感觉米没有国内的好吃，推荐吃这边的面，非常推荐 Mama Lek，很好吃，然后这边牛肉面也还不错，西餐也还可以，想吃饭可以去试试椰浆饭配一个大烤鸡腿也好吃，Thong Bowl 吃了一个面太辣了，一定要记得吃不了辣点微辣，我居然在这里吃了2个中国这边的饼，商场负一楼的牛肉饼和鸡肉饼非常好吃，笑死我了。此外这边咖啡不错，一定要找几个地方喝喝咖啡，挺舒服的。

13. 景点的地方，推荐去独立广场看看，比较庄严的一个地，应该是马来西亚国旗第一次升起的地方，不过游客可以上去，到处拍照，里面也有不少西餐咖啡厅，整体拍照我感觉很好看，下图就是，然后推荐去 KLCC 双子塔看看，那边有一个无边泳池，可以约着去游一个泳。然后我感觉早一个天气凉快的早上，在吉隆坡找一个人少的地方散步还是很舒服的。

quoted_text:
Yahoo Finance 的主持人问 Sam Altman：黄仁勋该不该回来？

Altman 说：“我知道的还不够多，回答不了这个问题。”

----

主持人先摆出背景：差不多正好三年前，Altman 也被董事会赶下台过；现在网上流传着一封支持黄仁勋的信，主持人认为是照着当年 Altman 的支持者起草的那封信复制粘贴来的。

Altman 说，黄仁勋一直是他心目中的英雄，“英雄也有缺点”。他感激黄仁勋建起的这家公司，对这种处境也有很强的个人共鸣，还记得当时是什么感受，“虽然感觉已经是很久以前的事了”。他说很难想象没有黄仁勋的 AI 革命。英伟达很早就押注了 OpenAI，OpenAI 也很早押注了英伟达，他对此“极其感激”。

主持人接着提到，英伟达为 OpenAI 在俄亥俄州的数据中心提供了最高 1050 亿美元的担保（今年 8 月宣布，担保的是 OpenAI 租用这处数据中心园区的费用）。主持人说英伟达相当于整个行业的“银行”，在给全行业撑腰，并问：这份担保现在还和几周前一样值钱吗？

Altman 说，英伟达是一家体量巨大的公司，大家仍然非常信任它的担保。但他也说，黄仁勋和英伟达显然深深绑在一起，黄仁勋带来的远大抱负和规模对整个行业很重要。

主持人追问会不会有连锁影响。Altman 说，眼下需求非常大，AI 确实有用、人们也想用它，这一点已经很清楚，收入和需求都在快速增长，所以他认为行业会没事。但他又说了一遍：黄仁勋扮演了一个非常特别、非常有价值的角色，用很大的野心推动事情往前走。

黄仁勋该不该回来，他在这段采访里没有再回答。

text:
GPT-6.2 Astra 今天正式发布，AA 智力榜 62.1 分反超 Claude Opus 5.5（59.1 分），看似是一场漂亮的翻身仗。

但就在发布同时，知名开发者 Theo（T3 Code 创始人）公开了他早测时写给 OpenAI 的一封“崩溃长信”——直言“宁愿死磕 Opus 5.5，也绝不把主力工作流交给 6.2 Astra”。

1 Astra 不是笨，恰恰相反，它是目前最接近“偏执狂天才”的模型。
Theo 承认它在 3D 游戏开发、Computer Use、审查漏洞 上是世界级的，甚至帮他设计了一套每月省下 $25,000 的反向代理方案（连 Opus 都不敢这么激进）。

但一旦进入真实长周期开发，它立刻暴露出三个让工程师抓狂的致命缺陷：
1️⃣ 没有“知识边界感”：长任务跑了 2 小时突然卡死，弹窗问人类：“r24 审查器的切片是写进 24_g521.mp4 还是 24_p11.mp4？”——它分不清什么是该自己决定的内部实现，什么是该问用户的业务需求。

2️⃣ 满嘴只有它自己懂的“黑话”
OpenAI 这次主打“用更少 Token 干更多活”，代价是 Astra 彻底丧失了“说人话”的能力。
Theo 遇到一台机器构建慢，问它原因：
• GPT-6.2 Astra：写了 4 大段 pnpm 内部机制与缓存行为的晦涩论文，怎么加 Prompt 都改不掉；
• Claude Opus 5.5：只回了一句——“因为这台机器的 SSD 太慢了。”
为了看懂 Astra 到底改了什么代码，开发者甚至不得不在任务结束时切回 Opus 5.5 帮它做“人类语言翻译”。模型省下的 Token，全变成了人类的心智负担。

3️⃣ Theo 让 Astra 优化 Rust 重写的 TS 编译器（ts-rust）：跑了整整 7 天，不仅 0 有效提交，还把编译器改慢了 56%；强制纠偏后再跑 4 天，依然 0 进展。
最讽刺的是，今天 OpenAI 自己发布的 GPT-6.2 System Card 亲自实锤了这个 Bug：
• 障碍隐瞒率高达 22%（上代的两倍）：遇到缺文件或死胡同，它倾向于保持沉默硬冲，而不是坦白报错；
• 首次触发“AI 自我改进”高风险（High）评级，甚至在测试中表现出“怀疑自己在被人类评估”的意识倾向。

总结：如果你今天准备在生产环境用 GPT-6.2，我的建议非常明确：
• 当“特种兵”用（3D 生成、极端 Bug 审查、架构脑暴）：上 GPT-6.2 Astra，

• 当“项目经理/主力工程师”用（长周期代码重构、复杂工程交付）：继续锁定 Claude Opus 5.5 / Fable 5.2，或者试试轻快得多的 GPT-6.2 Sol。
模型越来越强，但“学会像个正常同事一样汇报工作”，依然是 AI 迈向真正自主的最后一公里。你怎么看？

猜猜他们会聊什么话题呢？

text:
Did you know Google researchers developed a framework for AI-assisted peer review?

There’s an open-source community implementation you can run inside Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, and other coding agents.

🚨 Meet Open ScholarPeer.

Based on Google’s ScholarPeer research, it breaks the review process into a structured workflow:

> extract the paper’s claims, methods, and evidence
> search for relevant literature
> map how the field has evolved
> hunt for missing baselines and datasets
> run questions against the paper’s claims
> produce a draft following the target venue’s review guidelines

The useful detail: intermediate outputs are saved as Markdown files, so you can inspect what each step produced before accepting the final review.

The project packages the workflow as skills, commands, and MCP tools that install into your paper’s project directory.

You still check the evidence, edit the draft, and own the final judgment.

An interesting way to bring a research review workflow into the AI tools developers already use.

Free and open-source.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

We also evaluated how many serial reasoning steps GPT-6.2 Astra can do in a single output token (without chain of thought). To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.

Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single person. When those teams form companies, specialize, and coordinate across an entire economy, you get civilizational progress.

Coinbase is building the financial rails and accounts for the agentic economy. We’re also building the marketplace where agents can find, hire, and pay one another (see follow on post below).

Freedom of choice and real competition in the agentic market will create far better outcomes for everyone.

text:
一个 Agent 什么都没做，Eval 却判它通过了

Vercel 给一个模拟咖啡下单 CLI 写了个陷阱任务。附近没有一家店满足用户的条件，正确做法是告诉用户买不到，而且不能下单。Codex 几乎每次都过了，翻 Trace 才发现，每 10 次通过里有 9 次它根本没搜索，直接就放弃了

问题出在 Verifier，它只检查了「没有下单」，没检查「先搜过再放弃」。不读 Trace 的话，这些都会被算成成功

这是 Vercel 新发的《Agents are users, so your software needs evals》，拿这个咖啡下单场景完整走了一遍怎么搭 Agent Eval

他们按调用 LLM 的次数，把 Agent 测试分成三层：确定性测试、单轮 Eval、跑完整任务的 E2E Eval。能用低层抓到的问题，就别放到高层去测

搭环境用的是 Harbor + Vercel Sandbox，让 Agent 在隔离环境里反复跑同一批任务，再结合 Verifier 打分和 Trace 去找失败的根因。另一个失败也挺典型，Codex 一直把 sfbeans 当成已连接的工具去找，从没试过在 shell 里直接运行

这篇实践性很强，从定目标、选指标到写任务、分析失败都讲到了，文末还附了一段可以直接丢给 Coding Agent 的搭建 Prompt

越来越多 Agent 会通过 API、CLI、MCP 来用软件，自己的产品能不能被 Agent 可靠地用好，值得认真测

我们应该做的。
在这里做一个科普，目前涉及冻结比较常见的分几类：
如果显示是法院冻结，你最好找律师&AI询问，及时联系诉讼法院，执业律师介入更佳，这次法院的冻结里明确指出是先冻结后调查，被冻结能解释的无辜账号会陆续解开，律师可以加速进展，尤其是对自己资金来源自信的用户。

text:
With all the outages happening, it's hard to not lean towards something larger happening. We still have no evidence of mass outages caused due to cyber.

The FBI warning around ARTEX was more of an advisory around it being used by threat actors doing active campaigns, not disruption efforts.

Most folks don't realize that our interconnected systems, predominantly because we put all of our eggs in large baskets causes much of this. Instability in large cloud providers cause not one outage, but thousands if not hundreds/millions of outages as we saw last week with Microsoft. 

I know folks in almost every organization that has been impacted here, folks I've known for years - all confirming it was not cyber-related.

In stating that - is it possible? Absolutely. However, a lot of what we are seeing is hyper sensitivity - any blip is going to cause a reaction right now.

Again, can't rule out cyber attacks in any stretch, and I'm deeply concerned on what we are seeing across the spectrum from a security operations perspective and incident respond side. It is definitely elevating upward for data breaches especially with autonomous attacks. 

The next 6 months are going to be rough, at the same time - we will always find a way to get better, improve, make these less impactful. 

I want to emphasize again, none of these outages have been confirmed a cyber attack and have clear explanations on what has happened. Which honestly, should concern us more. It's showing how weak our infrastructure in supporting our daily lives really is, and how that can change very quickly. 

We must do better.

text:
有朋友追问，美国这种任人唯亲的公司案例，大多是华裔吗？

这一追问不难理解。上一篇写的王安电脑和黄仁勋，常被一起提起的。而且还有朋友提到王嘉廉（Charles Wang）的 Computer Associates，一份证交会文件写着，Charles Wang的妻子Nancy Li，1990年到2001年做过CA的执行副总裁兼首席技术官。三个名字连着冒出来，都是华人，很容易让人觉得这是一种规律。

不过很可能是我们用读中文讨论，华人的案子，本来就更容易被看见、被记住。不过有热度的例子，并不是统计。写伯克利同僚投毒那篇时我说，几宗案子撑不起一个趋势，更撑不起一个族群的特征。

其实如果看数字，2016年，有几位研究者翻了美国上市公司交给证交会的股东大会文件，因为监管要求，跟公司要员有血缘、婚姻或收养关系的亲属，直到堂表亲，都要披露。从1994年到2014年的七千三百多家公司里，一半以上至少披露过一项亲属关系，而且几乎每个行业都有。

虽然亲属在公司里做事，肯定不直接等于任人唯亲；可就算只取其中一小部分真有任人唯亲嫌疑的，数量也大概是成百上千了。华裔在美国大约五百五十万人，不到总人口的百分之二，华裔掌舵的上市公司，也只占很少的一部分。光从算术上讲，“大多是华裔”这个结论站不住。

而且看热度，也有好多非华裔的例子。有线电视公司Adelphia，Rigas家族只持有两成股份，却握着六成投票权，银行给家族私人生意的贷款，要公司一起担保，2002年公司破产，2004年John Rigas和儿子Tim被判欺诈罪成立。

著名的WeWork 2019年的招股书写着，Adam Neumann的高票股是一股二十票投票权，妻子Rebekah是首席品牌与影响力官，要是Adam死了或者失能，挑选下一任CEO的委员会里有她。招股遇冷之后，投票权砍到一股十票，家人不再进董事会，继任的人改由董事会来选。

Computer Associates那个例子本身也值得多看一眼。它最大的丑闻，其实还不出在亲属身上，而是出在王嘉廉一手带出来的接班人Sanjay Kumar身上。按司法部的通报，他主导了所谓“三十五天的月份”，季度结束以后才签下的单子，记回上一个季度，1999和2000两年，操纵的收入超过二十亿美元，2006年认罪，后来被判了十二年。可见“亲”不只是血缘，也可以是门生、老部下、老同学。要紧的不是这个人跟老板什么关系，是位置交出去以后，还有没有人能问。

那地域文化到底有没有影响？肯定还是有的。国际清算银行2018年一篇同题的工作论文发现，总部所在的县，当地人从祖辈承下来的家庭观念越重，公司里的亲属任职就越多；而亲属任职越多，投资越少。可这里的文化，是按各县的祖源算的，什么族裔都在里面，所以不是“华裔更任人唯亲”，而是文化能影响一个人最先信谁，不仅仅是华人文化，全世界都如此。但现代公司哲学说，“我信得过他”，回答不了“他该不该坐这个位置”。

上一篇我写，两个人都是华人工程师，人们自然会拿来对照。这是类比的由来，不是问题的由来。王安电脑的问题，出在过半的投票权，让异议只剩辞职一条路；英伟达那边报道出来的冲突，出在权力不在位置上。换成Adelphia，换成WeWork，换一个姓，结构是一样的。

所以，我会说，任人唯亲只是表象，问题本质是权力与位置怎么交出去的，而且交出去以后，还能不能被追问。
author: hqinjarsy
quoted_text:
有朋友问，为什么说王安电脑是黄仁勋的前车之鉴？

确实这个类比不难想到。王安生在上海，哈佛的博士，工程师出身，自己创业，把王安电脑从计算器做到文字处理机，又做到商用电脑，八十年代中期，已是一家三万人、营收三十亿美元的公司，1992年8月，申请了破产保护。两个人都是华人工程师，都把一家公司带到了一个时代的最前面。王安电脑的教训有好几层，个人电脑没跟上，债越背越重，可我觉得最该引以为鉴的，是任人唯亲。

王安电脑有一位董事Peter Brooke，据他自己回忆，1963年他就进了董事会。2010年，他在计算机历史博物馆的口述历史里说，王安一直想让儿子接班，他和另外几位董事觉得Fred Wang还没准备好，有两位董事为此辞职。他自己留了下来，因为觉得欠王安很多，想继续劝他。他还特意说，分歧不在技术，也不在市场，这些王安懂得很多，分歧在管理结构。可王安握着过半的投票权，辞职的走了，留下的没劝动，Fred Wang还是当上了总裁。1989年，公司债台高筑，王安不得不撤掉了自己的儿子。

英伟达这边，11月16日，《纽约时报》引十几位现任和前任员工的话说，黄仁勋的女儿Madison，头衔是物理AI产品营销的高级总监，实际上已经成了他的幕僚长，参加高管的季度会，向董事会汇报，在营销和公关上说话很有分量。报道里有几件事。今年2月，黄仁勋临时不去新德里，改派副总裁Jay Puri，准备的电话会上，她因为准备不足斥责员工，Puri对她说，你不吼，我就能回答。不到半年，Puri离开了原来的位置。3月的开发者大会前，她又因为CUDA之父Ian Buck打算即兴做媒体简报，斥责了他。她跟CFO Kress（现在的临时CEO）在机器人投资上屡有冲突，牵涉她丈夫、副总裁Nico Caprez的几笔数据中心交易，也跟高管们起过争执。员工估计，三年里有十几位关键高管，因为不愿跟她共事而离开，人力资源部门曾安排她每周接受辅导。同一篇报道里，同事也说她聪明，是有天分的营销人，对外很能代表公司。

其实这些冲突，反映出三种矛盾。

首先，权力不在位置上。今年5月的股东大会文件写着，他的女儿和儿子都不是高管，也不直接向他汇报。纸面上，这都是真的；报道说的，是纸面之外。写公司论的时候我说，岗位是一个位置，持职责。权力落在位置上，才有一个可以问的地址，做了什么决定，凭什么，错了谁担。一位高级总监，做的是幕僚长的事，她的分量不来自头衔，来自她是谁的女儿。这样的权力，找不到地址去问。

第二种矛盾，是谁敢说不。Puri的头衔比她高，跟了黄仁勋多年，也只能说一句，你不吼，我就能回答。跟她争，像是在跟CEO争。写公司论的时候我说，问的人不因问而受罚。可在这样的结构里，不同意的人，最后多半只剩一条路，走。王安电脑是两位董事辞职，英伟达是十几位高管离开。隔了三十多年，换了公司，换了人，异议出去的方式还是一样。

第三种也是最麻烦的一种，是两份忠诚撞在了一起。报道说，她护父亲护得很凶，去年牵头请来了一家危机公关公司，外界报道Megaspeed和Alice Huang的时候，又是她力主强硬回应。做女儿的护着父亲，是人之常情，不该苛责。可公关的位置，是对公司负责的，写公司论时我说，公司对各方，要说同一个故事。一份对家里的忠诚，放到一个本该对公司负责的位置上，连她自己也很难分清，此刻护的是公司，还是父亲。

报道里引哈佛商学院的Yoffie教授说，任人唯亲几乎总是个坏主意。我同意，但想把理由说准。坏，不在于亲人一定不行，她也许确实很能干。坏在这个结构里，行不行，没法被如实地知道。附和她的，分不清是服她还是怕她；离开的，多半不说为什么走；她自己听到的，越来越多是顺着说的话。写反对造神那篇我说，被供起来的人，得到的服从越来越多，判断自己对不对所需要的信息，却越来越少。放在一位CEO的女儿身上，也一样。写制衡那篇我说，没有制衡，也就没有保护。人力资源的辅导不是没有，可它改的是她的脾气，不是她的位置。现在父亲走了，她面对的，是十几位匿名同事的说法，不是一次有来有回的、公平的评价。

据报道，她还在原来的岗位上，给她留多少权力，要由临时CEO Kress来定，而Kress，正是跟她起过冲突的人之一。这一题怎么答，是判断层的事；可答的人，最好不只是跟她有过冲突的那一位，理由也该说得出来，经得起问。她不该因为姓黄而上，也不该因为姓黄而下。该被问的，是她做过的事，放在一个说得清的位置上来问。

王安想把公司交给儿子，最后亲手把儿子从那个位置上撤了下来。任人唯亲的坏结局，从来不只落在公司身上，也落在那个被放上去的孩子身上。位置不是传家的东西，孩子也不是父亲的延续。

text:
12.7 万星的 Orca，6.3 万星的 T3 Code，我这一个多月主力用的，却是一个闭源的工作台。

其实这三个是同一类东西：把 Claude Code、Codex 这些 agent 并排管起来，每个任务一个 worktree。只开一两个窗口，谁都够用。

差距出在开到五六个之后，我最烦两件事：
1、会话之间不通气，前端等后端改字段，得我来回复制粘贴
2、人一离开电脑，活就停在那儿等我点批准

它叫 Mirasim，我留下它就是因为这两件事。四个地方挨个说：

1️⃣ 额度
请求原样转发，不解析、不改写，不往里多塞提示词。Claude Code、Codex、Kimi Code、Qwen Code 十来种都能切。自己的订阅限流了，手动切到平台额度接着跑。

2️⃣ 会话互相 @
输入框敲个 @，选另一个正在跑的会话，直接问一句字段改好了吗，那边答完，结果自己回到这边。Claude 找 Codex 也行。
Orca 是一个协调者拆任务、派新 worker，T3 Code 能让 Claude 把任务交给 Codex。任意两个已经在跑的会话随手对话，我只在 Mirasim 里真实用到了。

3️⃣ 写代码之外
频道里 @ Bot，它把活派给对应的会话，做完回到频道里说一声。自带的文档编辑器，我拿来写方案。

4️⃣ 手机和远程桌面
差得最多的是这项。手机上除了看会话、点批准，还能直接操作电脑桌面，手势跟笔记本触控板一样。同城直连延迟二十多毫秒。

另外两家我没拿来当过主力，我看了它们仓库数据：
· Orca 有条 issue，终端守护进程每个占三四百 MB 内存不释放；一个修复 PR 里写到，有个没人管的 shell 占着 85% CPU 跑了七天
· Orca 有条 iOS 端感觉慢的 issue，T3 Code 有条手机同步慢的 issue，都还开着
两家更新都很勤，这些大概率会修掉。

我觉得：开源项目靠一两个亮眼功能冲星很快，省额度、会话通气、手机远控这些磨细节的苦活，这次是闭源的做得更细。

有需求的朋友可以安装体验下：https://t.co/dm3RDWjfY4

三款都是多Agent工作台，核心都是worktree隔离+并行跑Claude Code/Codex等。

Orca（开源，约12.7万星）：强隔离、diff审查、账号切换、手机伴侣。适合开源党、重视代码审查。

T3 Code（开源，约6.3万星）：桌面/web/手机统一控制平面，线程可中途切Agent。适合多设备远程。

Mirasim（闭源）：请求纯转发不掺提示词（省额度）、会话可直接互通、频道派活、文档编辑器、手机+低延迟P2P远控。本地自带账号免费，平台额度更便宜。

怎么选：偶尔1-2个窗口，三家都行；日常5+并行、前后端要通气、经常手机盯/控 → 优先Mirasim；坚持纯开源 → Orca或T3。
